speechtext:
I am speaking to the point
of order raised and I desire to call the attention of the house to one precedent. In 1926, when the present government was in opposition, I find the following action taken by the house. It was moved by the then hon. member for Cape Breton North-Victoria (Mr. L. W. Johnstone), that leave *be granted under rule 39 to adjourn the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, to call the attention of the house and the government to the acute distress existing among the coal miners 
of Nova Scotia, many of whom were actually on the verge of starvation. My motion follows almost word for word the motion made in 1926.
I might state also that in the speech from the throne delivered in 1926, reference was made to the conditions in Nova Scotia, as follows:
W itli a view to affording such remedies as may appear to be practical and appropriate, the government also propose to appoint a royal commission to inquire fully into the claims that the rights of the maritime provinces in regard to the operation of the Intercolonial railway have not been observed, and that in regard to transportation, immigration and other economic factors these provinces have suffered prejudicially, in their position under confederation.
At that time the condition of the miners in Nova Scotia was not a matter of recent occurrence. I would draw the attention of the house to the fact that in 1926 this motion was made during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. My motion is on almost all fours with the motion made in 1926, and I submit that I should be allowed to proceed.
No direct reference is made in the speech from the throne this year to any action which the government intends to take to deal with unemployment. We should not at this time insist on technicalities as I consider there is no more important question to be dealt with by parliament. The speech from the throne makes a certain vague reference to the economic conditions which prevail at the present time but there is no reference at all to any definite action which the government intends to take in order to meet the existing situation. In the rules of procedure the word "definite" is used, and we have to deal with a definite rather than an indefinite matter. May I point out also that the appropriations which the government has voted will expire to-day and there will be no further funds available for the municipalities or the provincial governments with which to cope with the present conditions.
Therefore, I consider thare is an urgent need for a discussion of this question which, as I have stated before, I believe to be the most important question that can come before this house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking on
the point of order it seems to me that this matter involves the rights of the members of this house. In stating the procedure subsection 3 of standing order 31 reads as follows:

Unemployment
He then hands a written statement of the matter proposed to be discussed to Mr. Speaker, who, if he thinks it in order, and of urgent public importance, reads it out and asks whether the member has the leave of the house.
If objection is taken, Mr. Speaker requests those members who support the motion to rise in their places and, if more than twenty members rise accordingly, Mr. Speaker calls upon the member who has asked for leave.
I submit that the mover of this resolution (Mr. Heaps) has complied with the rules. He has handed to the Speaker a written statement of the matter proposed to be discussed.
I realize that the next clause of the standing order is to the effect that if the Speaker thinks it in order it is read out, but I take it that that is only a formal matter. The proposed motion might not be formally in order; then it is for you, Mr. Speaker, to say that it is not in order and to reject it. But we are here dealing with another matter. With all deference to Your Honour I do not think it can be said that thd possibility of the introduction of a motion of this kind is dependent upon the decision of Your Honour as to what is an urgent matter; that is dependent upon the twenty hon. members who may rise and support it. I do not think there can be any question that the motion is formally in order. Several years ago a motion in precisely the same form was introduced upon a like occasion and no question was raised by the Speaker as to its being out of order. A precedent was established and I do not see how it can be said that this is not in order. The only ground upon which he can rule that it is not in order is as to whether it is a relevant matter or not, and that depends on the decision of twenty members. I claim that it becomes your responsibility, Mr. Speaker, to ask whether or not twenty members believe that this is a matter of urgent public importance.
The suggestion has come from the opposite side of the house that already a reference along this line has been made in the speech from the throne. It must be conceded, however, that that is a very general reference, and my colleague has more than answered that when he has shown that similar action was taken on a previous occasion when the members of the present government were in opposition. As to the urgency of the matter-, may I emphasize that the grant runs out today and that already a number of municipalities are cutting off direct relief to large numbers of men and women? The municipalities take the ground that they have no help from the Dominion government. What is to be done in such a situation as that ? The Dominion government has given no indication of what its policy is to be and tomorrow these men will be on the streets. I have to-day from a western city a letter along that line.

speechtext:
This application is made under standing order 31, which reads:
(1)	Leave to make a motion for the adjourn-11lellj' I|le house (when made for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance) must be asked after the ordinary daily routine of business has been concluded and before notices of motions or orders of the day are entered upon.
(2)	The member desiring to make such a motion rises in his place, asks leave to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, and states the matter.
(3)	He then hands a written statement of the matter proposed to be discussed to the Speaker, who, if he thinks it in order and of urgent public importance, reads it out and asks whether the member has the leave of the house.
in the first place, before the matter is read to the house, the Speaker must consider that it is in order and of urgent public importance. Perhaps I cannot do better than to read to the house the written opinion I gave to the hon. member for North Winnipeg this morning when he kindly notified me that he was going to make this application.
I said:
Since discussing with you your proposal to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely-to call the attention of the house and the government to the acute distress existing among large numbers of industrial workers throughout the Dominion, I have carefully considered the same and it seems to me the matter to which you propose to call the attention of the house is now actually being discussed in the debate on the address, and is a matter specifically referred to in the third, fourth, fifth and sixth paragraphs of the speech from the throne and in the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition.
For the moment tile house lias laid aside the debate on the address to deal with supplementary estimates required for the administration of government. Within a few days the debate will be resumed and if the house considers that the matter you propose to call to its attention should be discussed forthwith, it has only to revert to the debate on the address for that purpose.
If it is suggested that the members now seeking to move the adjournment have already spoken in the debate on the address, I might point out that it is open to a member to move a sub-amendment to the amendment to the address and to then discuss the matter, and that when the amendment now before the house is disposed of there will be a further opportunity to speak on the main motion.

In support of this decision I would quote May's Parliamentary Practice, 13th edition, page 248:
Slotion for adjournment regarding matters for the discussion of which the committee of supply or other appointed business-
The appointed business in this case being the debate on the address:
-would afford an early opportunity, or a matter which is under the consideration of a select committee, have been ruled to be out of order.
I therefore rule that the motion is out of order on the ground as stated in that letter, and on the ground taken by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) under paragraph (c) of section 6 of rule 31. That the motion anticipates a matter which has been previously appointed for consideration by the house, and particularly by the amendments to the address moved by the leader of the opposition.

I feel Mr. Speaker, that I would be recreant to my duty towards those people I represent in this house if I did not take the opportunity before the adjournment for Easter recess of drawing to the attention of the house some of the conditions which at the present time prevail in the Dominion of Canada. Those conditions are of such a nature that I feel parliament ought to take some definite action before we adjourn to-morrow. Following the adjournment a great many of us will be going back to our constituencies and will be meeting the people who sent us here. There is hardly a constituency in Canada at the present time which is not suffering from some form of economic distress. The first question which will be asked by our constituents and the first question we will face when we return to our home is, "What has parliament done to cope with the existing crisis?" Hon. members in this house with the possible exception of some members of the government, know nothing of What the cabinet has in mind to meet the conditions which now prevail. We had a special session of parliament. In July last year a change of government took place and at that time the opposition thought it was right and proper immediately after the election to summon the parliament to deal with the then very serious unemployment situation. sent emergency. This is the 31st day of March and money voted in September last practically ceases to exist because parliament is not in a position, except by another act to vote further sums of money. Apart from that, the whole of the $20,000,000 voted by parliament has been more or less used up by municipalities in dealing with the unemployment situation. At the present time, Mr. Speaker, I find a worse condition of unemployment in this country than I have ever known in the past. We could travel from the Atlantic to the Pacific and find these same deplorable conditions prevailing. I have before me certain communications to which I wish to refer to briefly. Here is one from Calgary which reads as follows. It is from the Mine Workers' Union of Canada:
In view of the deplorable conditions which exist in the mining industry throughout Canada.
Another one comes from the province of Nova Scotia. The statement is contained in a report of a special committee of a conference held on January 20 in Halifax. The report reads in part as follows:
Conditions of grave and calamitous unemployment have for some time existed and are at this time prevalent in the coal fields of Nova Scotia.
What else do we find? In the city of Vancouver 10,000 people have registered as being out of work. The number who have registered does not of necessity indicate the total number of people out of work because there are thousands who refuse to register but who nevertheless are unemployed. I could travel to Calgary, Edmonton and Winnipeg and find a similar condition. In the city of Winnipeg we have had more than 7,000 men who have been actually receiving relief from the city. In the cities of Fort William and Port Arthur the same deplorable conditions prevail. In the city of Toronto vast numbers of men are out of work. In fact only last week in that city a crowd of unemployed men looking for work were actually clubbed because they dared to look for jobs.
That is wrong.

Just a few day ago in the
city of Montreal a large number of unemployed men trooped into an office and the man in charge actually shot one of the men who oame in looking for work. Apparent!}' the man who did the shooting was afraid some harm might befall him. The man was shot right through his body.

These are the conditions prevailing throughout Canada, and I feel that this parliament ought not to adjourn for the Easter recess until the government brings down immediate measures to cope with the situation. The excuse may be offered that we have been in session only since March 12th. But there is no good reason why the house could not have met two months earlier to deal with the problem. If parliament could have met in September in an emergency session there is no reason why it could not have met at the ordinary time this year so that we could have done something to meet existing conditions.
In the last session of parliament the government adopted three measures which they claimed would in some way alleviate or possibly put an end to unemployment in this Dominion. I never expected for one moment that the party now in power could end unemployment, and I am not going to blame them if they do not end unemployment in this country. The only blame I attach to this government 'is that hon. members opposite made such wild and rash promises to the electors, representing that they were the only ones who could solve the problem.
I have said that we could have met much sooner so that we might have dealt with the unemployment situation. I was very sorry indeed, Mr. Speaker, when a few weeks ago I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) what action the government intended to take to meet this serious state of affairs, the only reply I received from the right hon. gentleman-and then it was only after he had been requested by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) to do so that he replied- was that I should put the question on the order paper. I was to put the question on the order paper and then it might be answered. That may be a way of evading a question, but it is not the way to reply to an important question asked in the House of Commons. If the Prime Minister had answered my question in the way in which a question of that kind should be answered, I might probably not have found it necessary to get up in my place to-day and insist upon some action on the part of the government. When the Prime Minister of the government evades the answering of such a question, it seems to me the only resource we members have is to bring to the attention of parliament and the country the situation as it actually exists. In fact, when the Prime Minister made that reply to the question I asked him, he said he was going to follow dn the footsteps of the former

Unemployment-Mr. Heaps
government. Now that is a rather unusual attitude for a Conservative Prime Minister to take in this house. But I have noticed of late how eager the Prime Minister is to follow Liberal practices. Upon his return from the Imperial conference be intimated that he was following in the footsteps of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier. And when the right hon. gentleman was in opposition he used to quote continually from Lord Morley's Life of William Ewart Gladstone. He seems to have quite a tender spot for such quotations, a desire to follow in the path of Liberals of the past. I sincerely trust, however, that the Prime Minister will not follow entirely in what the Liberal party has done in the past, but will branch out into new lines in order to meet the problems we have, with new ideas, because the old ideas cannot solve the problems of to-day. It is no use attempting to deal with twentieth century problems with nineteenth century ideas; it cannot be done.
In September last the government -had three proposals for dealing with the unemployment situation. The first was the prevention of dumping into Canada. That was one of their proposals and it became law. But not only did it become law; the government took upon themselves the right and prerogative which for many years parliament has exercised There is therefore no excuse to-day that foreign goods are coming into competition with Canadian manufactures. That, as I say, was one remedy. The second remedy was the voting of 820,000,000 to give immediate relief where that was thought necessary. And the $20,000,000 more or less has been spent. Now I want to lay down, first, the maxim that capital expenditures are no remedy for unemployment. In fact, the more capital expenditures are made for unproductive works, the more we aggravate an already serious situation. Consequently the mere voting of sums of money for the carrying on of certain public works will in no way settle the problem of unemployment. Now we come to the third remedy offered by the government-and this was their trump card. They claimed that if the tariff were raised extremely high so as to prevent the importation of goods it would * provide work for people at home and practically solve the unemployment problem. Today, after about six months' experience, we find that none of these so-called remedies are in any way a solution for unemployment.
I wish to show, by the figures supplied by the government, the extent of unemployment in Canada at present. I find there were 228,351 persons who received work as a result of the emergency vote passed by parliament last September. They worked a total of 22110-30
3,975,355 days; that is to say, they worked on an average, approximately 18 days during the last five or six months. Now, the average wage they would receive from those who employed them would be approximately $60. In other words, they earned an average of S60 under the emergency legislation passed last year. What do we find further? In addition to the numbers who received work, there were also large numbers who received relief by way of groceries, meals and so forth.
I find on page 11 of the report of 1931, dealing with the unemployment situation that there were 49,946 families and 64,728 individuals who received relief. In other words, over 130.000 persons received direct relief in addition to the 208,351 persons who were given employment during the past few months. This will give some indication of the serious unemployment situation which exists to-day.
I find that the index for employment on August 1, 1930, was 118.8, and on February 1, 1931, it had dropped to 100.7. If we deduct only a proportion of the number of people who were employed on emergency work, working under some form of government assistance, we find that in that same period the drop in unemployment was in the neighbourhood of 30 per cent-certainly a very grave state of affairs and one that demands the attention of parliament. Then we have to consider the vast numbers of men who at present are on part time employment. We find that throughout this country men who formerly worked on full time are working three or four days per week, and they have a most difficult struggle to make both ends meet. What have the unemployed to look forward to? In previous years, in the spring men would look forward to being able to go on the farms and find employment in that way. This year those men will not be able to do so; in fact I am inclined to believe that instead of men going from the cities to the farms there will be people coming from the farms to the cities to look for work. Consequently the already bad situation which prevails in our industrial centres is likely to become much worse through that reverse movement. I find, Mr. Speaker, that in the few times the Prime Minister has spoken in public since the emergency session of last September he has made special reference to what he would do if the conditions were not changed when parliament again met. Speaking in Regina on December 30, the Prime Minister said:
I tell you that when parliament meets, if there is not then evident further increase in employment, additional steps will be taken to meet the situation.



Unemployment-Mr. Heaps
I believe, Mr. Speaker, we have a right to know what those additional steps are to be.
If any.

Yes, as the hon. member for Bow River says, what additional steps there are to be, if any. The hundreds of thousands of men and women who at present are out of work and who are marching through our streets in demonstrations, men and women who are hungry and many of whom are starving, have their eyes fixed on this parliament, and they expect us here to take some action that will in some way deal with this very pressing problem. At the present time, on this 31st day of March, we do not know what parliament is likely to do in an attempt to meet thie situation, and we are not likely to meet again until April 13. There is involved in this question something which I regard as of very great importance. As I have already said, I believe there is no question that ought to challenge the attention of members of this house and the attention of parliament collectively more than the question of unemployment, yet I see scant attention paid to-day to this important problem. I noticed that When my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) spoke on this question recently practically the whole Conservative party walked out of the house, and it just makes me wonder how much hon. members really care for the men and women who happen to be out of work and suffering at the present time. When my hon. friend from South Vancouver (Mr. Maclnnis) spcke on the same question he was met in exactly thie same way; he found complete indifference to the suffering of our fellow-Canadians.
Yo-u never propose anything.

It is for the government to bring proposals before the house, and when the government will come to the house with concrete proposals I will be willing to give them all the support of which I am capable, if I believe those proposals will help the situation. If the government will listen to what I have to tell them and will adopt my proposals, they may be equally sure of my support, and perhaps before I get through to-day I will bring forward a few suggestions which they might do well to adopt.
But there are only forty-six members of the Conservative party to listen even now.

Well, that is nearly three times as many as were here when my hon. 
friend from Winnipeg North Centre spoke the other day. When the hon. member for South Vancouver dealt with this question he was met with jeers by hon. members opposite when he attempted to tell of the sufferings of the unemployed in the city of Vancouver. It is all right for the party in opposition to show sympathy for the men and women out of work, but it seems another matter when that party happens to attain power.
There is a rather strange coincidence which came to my notice to-day, Mr. Speaker. On March 31 of last year I rose in my place to call the attention of parliament and particularly of the government to this question of unemployment. On that day I brought forward a motion asking the government to take immediate steps to deal with the then existing unemployment situation. The Conservative party was in opposition at that time, and the opposition benches were pretty well filled on that occasion. There were no jeers, and there was no question of my bringing forward certain proposals. The Conservative party insisted on the government of the day bringing in their proposals to deal with unemployment, and I hope that party to-day will be just as consistent in their attitude and will take immediate action to deal with the situation.
I said this parliament had a collective duty in connection with this question. We have a responsibility, and we cannot evade it either individually or collectively. The main responsibility, however, naturally rests with the government, and the responsibility of the government is to deal with this very grave menace that is confronting us. We must bear in mind that the people of this country look upon this parliament to govern, but if we allow hundreds of thousands of workers and their dependents to go without the bare necessities of life I want to ask you, Mr. Speaker, what kind of confidence, if any, can -those people have in our parliamentary institutions. I claim that the very fitness of this parliament to govern the country under such circumstances is at stake to-day. If we do not live up to our responsibilities we will deserve everything the people of this country may hurl at us.
We claim that we are living under a form of political democracy; I have heard the Prime Minister speak about the dignity of parliament and the respect with which it should be looked upon by the people throughout this country. The degree of respect we receive from the people of this Dominion will be only in proportion to the way in which

Unemployment-Mr. Heaps
we give the people the things to which I claim they are fully entitled. I want to say in all seriousness that parliament is losing its grip upon the people, because while we have . a form of political democracy we have allowed to grow up side by side with it a financial autocracy, which to-day is more powerful than the democracy. The question now arises whether we are to be subordinate to these economic forces which seem to have a strangle hold upon the very life of the millions of our people. That is the question, and to-day the problem arises, in dealing with the unemployment situation, what steps parliament will take to meet the conditions which exist throughout the country?
It has been claimed by some hon. members opposite that the unemployment situation is due first to the Liberal government which was previously in power, and secondly to the fact that certain economic conditions have been experienced throughout the world. To overcome the maladministration of nine years of Liberal rule, and to give additional employment to the workers of this dominion the Conservative party set about the task of increasing tariffs. If world conditions are responsible for unemployment no local application of a tariff will improve them; that goes without saying. If we are faced with world conditions, a tariff is no remedy for unemployment existing in Canada.
It would seem that the causes of unemployment lie far deeper than can be reached by a tariff and I think this matter should be considered from that angle. In our collective capacity as a nation we are not suffering from any shortage of goods; we have more than we know what to do with. Our elevators are choked with wheat and so much grain has been produced that it does not pay the farmer to ship because he will receive nothing for it. Yet, side by side with that condition, we have vast numbers of people in our cities who are without the bare necessities of life. How are we going to bring about a more equitable distribution of the goods produced? The tariff policy of the government is based upon the assumption that production must be increased. If production is increased how can the people consume that increased production if to-day they are unable to consume our present production? The great masses of the people must be given that purchasing power which will permit them to consume far more goods than they are allowed to at the present time. Production has been increasing by leaps and bounds for a number of years yet side by side with this enormous increase we find that the purchas-22110-304
ing power of the masses has remained practically stationary. If that purchasing power remains stationary and production increases it means that commodities will be piled up, and as that process continues sooner or later men find themselves out of work because they are unable to consume the goods they have produced.
Wages, based upon purchasing power, have remained practically stationary. To-day the human being is being exploited by the machine for the benefit of those who own the machine. Henry Ford said some little time ago that the machine was to be the slave of man. However, what has happened is that man has become the slave of the machine. From a governmental standpoint, we have not the faintest idea of'how to cope with this situation. It is claimed that the labourer is a partner in industry, but that is not so. He is only a drudge who receives a mere pittance for his labour.
I have been asked, what have we to offer as a remedy to meet the situation? I submit that capital to-day is taking too great a toll out of industry. If statistics were consulted I have no doubt that they would show that the amount of money paid out per annum in interest would equal the total payroll of the country. Unfortunately, we have not those statistics from our own Bureau of Statistics, but those of the United States show that that is the case. Industrial conditions in both countries are on a par, so the same would apply to Canada.
I claim that industry ought so to adjust itself as to guarantee to the labourer a fairly steady annual wage. At the present time a man receives so much per hour when there is work to be performed; if there is no work, he receives nothing. A man with $10,000 to invest receives an annual return on his investment and I claim, Mr. Speaker, that a human being who invests in industry all that he has to invest is entitled to an annual return. He is more deserving than is the man who invests a few thousand dollars.
In times of national emergency the government mobilizes our national resources. This is a time of great emergency with many thousands of our people facing starvation, it is an emergency for the meeting of which the government should mobilize all national resources. As I said before, we have in our warehouses more commodities than we know what to do with and side by side with that aggregation of wealth and commodities we have hundreds of thousands of Canadians who do not know where their next meal is coming from. That is the problem facing the government. It may be very well for the leader
Unemployment-Mr. Heaps

of this government to offer certain nebulous proposals as outlined in the speech from the throne, but what we need are definite proposals to meet the present situation. Something is said in the speech from the throne about returning to normal and prosperous conditions the like of which we have never seen in the past. Let me tell the right hon. the Prime Minister that such fine phrases as those contained in the speech from the throne will not fill one empty stomach. We want such action as will return us to the right kind of prosperity. We do not want a prosperity which is reflected in the bank clearings and in the annual statements of financial and industrial concerns, a prosperity affecting only the few and not the many. We do not want a prosperity which will make millionaires out of the few and paupers out of the millions. We want a prosperity which will give to the man on the farm and in our industrial centres a decent livelihood, a prosperity which will afford an opportunity for his children and all those dependent upon him and give that security of life which to-day is denied him.
To-day the responsibility is on the government The Prime Minister said that they were going to deal with the question or perish in the attempt. The time has come when he must deal with it, and although we are a small group, although there may be only three labour members in the house, we are to-day speaking for hundreds of thousands of people throughout the whole length and breadth of the Dominion. As hon. members know, when any matter arises pertaining to labour in various constituencies represented by members who are now in the house on the government side or the official opposition side, resolutions which are sent to those members are also sent to the Labour members. Those working people, whether they live in Nova Scotia or in the central provinces or in the western provinces, look to the small Labour group to bring these questions before the house, and as the government and the members generally deal with those questions, so shall they be judged by the working men and women in those constituencies.
When my colleagues, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and the hon. member for South Vancouver (Mr. Maclnnis) and I raise questions in the house, we feel that we are speaking for far more people than our own immediate constituents. By resolutions which have been sent to us and by dozens of letters which we have received, we know they are looking to us to raise this question; they are demanding

of us that we impress upon the government and the house the urgency of the matter. Therefore I hope the government will rise to the occasion, and will not deal with this question as if it were of no importance, for never has there been before the house a question of equal importance to that of unemployment at the present time. From coast to coast we have vast numbers of men asking for action from the government and I hope the government is not going to disappoint the workers or the agriculturists of this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
I should like to assure the
house that we have raised this question today, not with any desire to delay the ordinary business of the house, but because unemployment throughout the country at the present time is so serious that we could not allow the Easter holidays to pass without at least making an effort to have some definite pronouncement from the government with regard to what they intend to do in this matter. It may be very important that the estimates should be considered before the Easter holidays; it may be important that the contractors on the Welland canal should be paid, but it is equally important that the unemployed of this country should be cared for during the next two weeks.

A great
deal more important.

My hon. friend
from Bow River says that it is a great deal more important. I quite agree with him, because, after all, some of these contractors can manage in one way or another to get along for a few weeks. On the other hand, many of the unemployed are on the bread line and within a day or so they will be on the verge of starvation. It is tremendously important that this matter should be attended to without delay.
There are in the house members who claim to stand for the ancient rights of the British people. I am glad indeed that parliament has throughout the centuries permitted the ordinary members to voice their grievances before supply can be granted, and I am pleased we have this opportunity to-day of voicing what I believe are the real grievances of a large number of people in Canada.
When the question of the point of order and the introduction of the motion was before the chair, I ventured to say that I thought this matter was urgent and among other things I suggested that unless it were attended to, we might very easily have riots within the

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
next two weeks. I think those who have been in the house for any length of time will agree that I am not in any way inciting to riot, but I should like to point out that the very first responsibility of the government is to make such arrangements as will at least allow the people to live, to eat, and to-day there are many people who are not in a position, unless something is done in an organized way, even to obtain an existence. I am glad to notice many hon. gentlemen on both sides are giving attention to this matter to-day. I know quite well that as individual members they are very much interested in this subject and I would hope that a subject of this kind could be taken out of the range of party politics. I do not know how many other members feel about it, but the other day, although I have been in the house for ten years, I could not but be rather shocked at the levity that characterized the discussion on unemployment. It seemed to me that we were footballing it back and forth in order to obtain some party advantage and were not dealing with the question as its merits would warrant our doing. I know members individually would take a great deal of interest in any poor person who came to their doors, but a large majority of the members have not been quite so fully in touch with labour as some of us have, and from day to day they are perhaps not besieged as we are by unemployed people seeking relief. Under these circumstances I think they will pardon us if we stress more than they feel like doing, the importance of the question. Someone during my colleague's speech atempted to throw discredit upon his statement with regard to certain unemployed being clubbed. I happen to have in my hand a clipping from the Evening Citizen of March 28, 1931, and in it I find this statement contained in an editorial entitled "No Slave Labour in Canada.":
From Toronto, last Thursday, came word of the mayor's stand against the clubbing of unemployed men when they crowd eagerly before an unemployment portal in search of work.
I think no discredit should be thrown on the statement of my colleague. Further the editorial states:
In Montreal on. the same day, revolver shots were fired at a crowd of free but unemployed Canadian workers when they surged around the office of a private contractor.
The editorial proceeds in discussing these tvco news items, to say:
The wisdom of the law may have to be invoked in Montreal to determine how far the freedom of the Canadian workless is to be observed. They are free to starve, as this winter has demonstrated.
Again it says:
But the limit is being reached. The line is drawn at the portals of employment offices where men go to seek work. They must apparently be satisfied with freedom to starve. They cannot have employment. It is just a question how long this superior freedom of the Canadian workless can go on.
I do not think I need to spend much time to-day in stating the actual facts of the situation. In this corner we were glad last year to have the support of the Conservative party when we introduced the question of unemployment and urged that the government do something about the matter. The situation is worse to-day than it was a year ago. I think that will be frankly admitted. I am not going to discuss the question whether the onus for that should be placed upon the government or not. I do not think the government is primarily to blame for that, but I do say that if we obtained support from the Conservative party last year, we ought to obtain support this year when we introduce the question again and urge immediate action.
The conditions are worse.

Yes, the conditions are worse.
I do not propose to deal with the government's own report on the Unemployment Relief Act of 1930, but I would like to emphasize one statement made by my colleague, that we succeeded in providing for less than eighteen days' work, or three weeks' work, for the unemployed. Here was the special session called; we sat for two weeks and voted twenty million dollars for the relief of the unemployed. As a matter of fact, all that effort succeeded in providing only three weeks' work for a very limited number of individuals, 228,351, a smaller number than are now unemployed. That is an astonishing situation, that with all the effort we have made we have provided less than three weeks' work for less than the number of unemployed today.
In some way they have been looked after during the past winter. What is to happen after to-day when the relief is cut off? That is the emergency. I do not think we ought to go home for the Easter recess without provision being made to carry them for at least a few weeks longer because the ordinary spring work will not open up before that time and it should be remembered there will not be anything like the amount of spring work this year which there has been under normal circumstances.
I take just one or two items almost at random from the government's own report. In Manitoba, for example, there were 36,968

Unemploym.ent-Mr. Woodsworlh
individuals granted direct relief. I turn to tlie note at the bottom of that same table on page 11 of the report and read:
In addition to above, the city of Montreal reports having given 178.659 nights' lodgings to single men and 1,063,034 meals.
And so on. These extracts are simply indicative of the conditions that prevailed. If one wanted to go outside of the government's own reports, there are abundant evidences of the seriousness of the situation. There came to me the other day the March number of Social Welfare, a social workers' magazine, in which an account is given of what is being done by churches and philanthropic societies outside altogether of the aid which has been given by the government. One article concerns Winnipeg, and in this particular case includes what is being done by the government. It says:
The employment service of Canada reports no farm, camp or bush work, and the situation has been in the same condition since the early autumn of 1930. Since September 1, 1930, 4.012 married men have applied for assistance, 347 of whom have been placed in work on bridge and subway building, in which the provincial and Dominion governments participate, and 320 of whom have been given work in street cleaning, which is financed entirely by the city.
Or I turn to Montreal, and I find this statement by Dr. F. G. Pedley:
In the vicinity of Dufferin square, where five thousand idle men are registered, our slums are an eyesore to the community. Throughout the country there are countless level crossings where citizens of the Dominion are daily imperilled. In our own city there is great need for a subway to meet the ever-increasing traffic. The excuse that there is no work to do cannot stand in the face of these facts. If social work is to be constructive in this community and this country, it must careful}' consider ways and means to overcome such economic conditions as we are afflicted with this year.
I could turn to Hamilton or to the capital city itself, or Toronto. Let me quote a paragraph in regard to work that is being done by the United Church in the city of Toronto:
In these institutions 85,000 free meals were supplied, and 30,250 free beds provided. Clothing-including boots, socks, underwear, suits of clothes and overcoats, totalling many thousands-was distributed free to homeless men.
Take St. John, away down in the mari-times. From an article by Clarence Smith I quote:
On January 15, 728 men (25 non-residents) were registered, about 80 per cent of whom were day labourers. When the registrations at the labour unions' headquarters were added, between 1,000 and 1,100 was the estimated total. The population of Saint John is about 60,000.

I could proceed to read extracts from papers from coast to coast, but as I said I do not consider that it is necessary. We are all receiving daily, at least I am, letters and resolutions telling about the appalling conditions that prevail.
Now, what is being done? For one thing, the government is deporting a large number of the unemployed. Whilst I agree that it is a considerable relief to the individual municipalities to have these men deported, I think it is a serious state of things when men who have come to this country in good faith to settle here, and have attempted to get work, should be deported just because they are unable to get work. I have had scores of examples of that character. The way it is done is this: A man cannot get work, and he then either has to starve or commit a crime, or apply for relief. If he obtains relief, he is then a public charge, and on the ground of being a public charge he is deported. I think that is hardly fair to the immigrants that we have begged to come to this country. The older members of this house will remember that year after year I have stood in my place and protested against immigration to this country. I thought that we were bringing in more people than we could take care of. I thought these people were tending to crowd the local labour market, and that they themselves were being exploited. Now I urge that when the government has definitely adopted a policy of bringing people to this country and has definitely promised them work, as has been done through the various agencies, it is not for us immediately work is slack to deport them to the countries whence they came. Many of them have broken all their home ties in the old country. Many of them have spent all they had in order to pay for their passage to this country, and many of them would be excellent settlers if they got half a chance in this country. I would suggest that after we have spent millions of money in trying to advertise this country in Great Britain and Europe, it is, to say the least, very poor policy for us to return a great many of these disgruntled people to the old country suffering from what they regard, and I think rightly, as a substantial injustice. From that standpoint alone it seems to me we ought to look after these people.
There is a tendency at the present time to turn off all the single men. We have in the past had so many opportunities for work that it was considered that a single man could get out and rustle for himself. That is not true to-day. A single man is almost as help-

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
less as a married man so far as obtaining work is concerned. Of course, the unmarried group are a little more mobile and can drift more readily from place to place than can the married men, but it is no easier for them to get work. In fact, in nearly all our municipalities a preference is given, and perhaps quite rightly, to married men, but that means that when a single man is turned out of one city he simply drifts to another, and he finds it next to impossible to obtain work. I think of the situation as it was presented to me only a week or ten days ago when I happened to be back in my own city for a day or so. A young man whom I have known for several years came to see me. He was an Englishman. He had been employed on the provincial telephone lines. His work had stopped and he had been unable to obtain work since. He was forced to accept city relief. One day he objected to the treatment a fellow citizen was receiving. He considered the treatment was brutal and whether or not he was right he objected to it. As punishment relief was immediately cut off. "Now," he said, "what am I to do? I have not anything behind me; I have no resources whatever; the city refuses to give me relief; I am ostracized and I am driven to become a criminal." I gave him a small sum of money to tide him over for a day or two. I want hon. members to know that he was not begging but I gave him a small sum; then I came down to Ottawa. Mr. Speaker, I ask hon. members of this house what there is for that man to do? There is absolutely no work in the city for him; there is no work that he may get throughout the province. The only thing he can do is to smash a window.
No, no.
The only thing he can do is to become a criminal in order to live.
It is such members as my hon. friend who incite them to do it.
No, I am not inciting them.
Yes, my hon. friend is doing it right along.

No, I am not. I am putting .the predicament of that man before hon. members of this house and I ask what there is for a man in that position to do. In the city from which I come dtiring the last winter many men begged to be allowed to sleep in the jails, and they have done this for several years. Those conditions
were reported a year ago before our industrial relations committee in connection with the unemployment investigation. So we have it that this man is put into a position whereby he is forced to become a criminal in order to obtain anything to eat. I do not know what he is going to do. Of course he may beg. He is likely to be arrested for begging, because it is a crime. However, he is only one of hundreds across this country who find themselves in similar positions. If we go on in our present course without announcing any definite way to take care of these people there will be a great many people who will practically be forced into crime. After all it is a fundamental principle that people have the right .to live; I repeat, they have the right to live. Each person feels that right. For the life of me I cannot see how any government can claim the loyalty of individual citizens if it does not in some way provide for them a means of livelihood. In the absence of some such provision the very basis of organized government is swept away.
At this time I would like to call the attention of hon. members of this 'house to other classes who have not been provided Jor. Let us for instance consider the imperial veterans. We are endeavouring and are succeeding fairly well in providing for our own returned men. However, there are a great many people who were encouraged to come to this country after the war; they were imperial veterans. They came to our land with the intention of making it their home and for a year or two they did very well. Then there came the present depression. What are they to do? Our laws are not sufficiently wide to cover those people. Our own veterans are being cared for but the imperial veterans are not. Perhaps hon. members might say that they should look to Great Britain. However, they broke their relationships with the old land when they came to Canada. As individuals they are helpless. Hon. members can readily understand that the individual imperial veteran cannot write to Great Britain in the hope that he may receive relief. It would seem to me therefore that we should make special provision for the care of this group of people.
Then there is a large group of people who have been in the country for a period less than five years, or in individual cities for periods of less than one year. In many cases the period of one year is taken as the period necessary to establish residence. These people cannot be blamed because they found it necessary to drift from city to city. The fact is that a very large number of our
472	COMMONS
Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
transient labourers must move from plage to place to find work, so they cannot establish residence in any one city. The governing body of the individual city however feels that it is not under any responsibility to take care of such transients. I sympathize with the ratepayers of those cities. In the city of Winnipeg we have had thousands of people crowd in upon us from every quarter and we as citizens have felt that we have been asked to carry an unjust burden. Yet the indvidual unemployed transient is helpless; what is he to do? He has been in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and in a dozen places of northern Ontario getting jobs for short periods of time. In the proper sense of the term he cannot establish residence in any one of these places. I say it becomes necessary to take care of that group of people. Because of the fact that the relief is being cut off at the end of this month by a great many municipalities it seems to be that some provision should be made for those people, at least for the next few weeks.
The most serious aspect in this whole situation is the fact that the unemployed man is regarded as a near criminal. I take it that that mode of thinking is a relic of the old pioneer days in which most of us Canadians have been brought up. Undoubtedly in the old days any man who w-anted a job could readily find it. If he could not find it on his own farm he could go to that of his neighbour, and in those days they were anxious to have hired men. If he could not find employment on the farm he could go back to the bush; most of our people did go to the bush for several months during the winter. If a man could not find work in the city he could go out on construction work, but to-day construction work is very limited in extent. The days of the rapid building of our railroads are past. There are not the possibilities for work which existed at one time when the west was so rapidly opening up. Now, what are we to do under these circumstances? If a man cannot obtain work in Winnipeg he may-go to Regina, but he may probably find more unemployed men in Regina than there were in Winnipeg. He could go up to the Pas and as happened last spring he would find himself stranded with several other hundred men waiting to go up to Churchill. He may return from the Pas by freight train, as hundreds of them did, and go to Saskatoon. That is the situation with which we are faced today. Mr. Speaker, I do not believe we can

deal fairly with this question until we clear our minds of the conception we gained in our earlier pioneer days regarding unemployed men. We must recognize frankly that today it is not a crime to be unemployed; it is no crime whatever. It is not even an indication that a man is of low mentality, that he is lazy, useless or anything of that character. Many of our best men are caught at this time. That fact ought to be recognized and we ought to treat those unemployed men as self respecting citizens. Of course I would admit that if a man has some weakness, if he drinks or is lazy he might be the first to be turned off. The fact remains however that he has been doing work and that if suitable work were provided he would be at work again. I think we ought not to treat our unemployed men as criminals or near criminals.
I do not wish to expect too much from the government with regard to this question of unemployment. It may be true that the Prime Minister said that he would abolish unemployment. Well, if he expected to do that he was evidently mistaken; if the electors voted for him on that ground they also were mistaken. The very worst that can be said is that the government occupies its official position more or less under false pretences, or because they themselves were not apprised of the significance of the situation. I am not going to go into the political side of the question howe'er; probably we have had enough of that. To-day we are actually facing a very serious situation and I ask:	"What can be done
about it?" For several years we in this corner of the house have urged that provision should be made in the form of unemployment insurance. Unemployment insurance has been ridiculed as a dole. If one can properly interpret the speech delivered not long ago by the Minister of Labour (Senator Robertson) it would seem that we were not to have anything in the form of unemployment insurance in the near future. I have never suggested that unemployment insurance was a solution of our difficulties. The only solution is to find employment; and behind that, the still more fundamental problem the distribution of what is produced. But in the meantime I do suggest that unemployment insurance might help to tide over the present extremely critical situation. It has been despised as the dole; but I submit that nothing is more degrading than our present system, or lack of system, in providing relief. This practice of turning people out into the streets

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
to stand in queues before soup kitchens; turning them out to beg until they are passed over to some mission which may keep them overnight; this practice that prevails in my own city, of giving relief tickets and sending men to all sorts of places to tide them over a day or so-this is all absolutely demoralizing. I ask the government therefore to consider most seriously the question whether it would not be possible in the near future to institute some form of unemployment insurance.
I do not want to be hypocritical in suggesting this, because I know the difficulties with which the government would be confronted. This is not a time when there could be any reserve piled up through contributions. We are in a period when the majority of people think it is a time to economize. I do not agree with that policy, but the majority of people take that position. I know the government would face grave difficulties in instituting unemployment insurance at this time. More than that, I am doubtful-and I say it frankly-whether unemployment is not so great that it would almost swamp the resources of any government that might attempt to relieve it in any adequate form. Nevertheless, it is at the same time incumbent on the administration of the day at least to make an effort to do something of this character, even though a full-fledged scheme might not be feasible.
Some of us perhaps are a little handicapped in advocating reforms of this kind, simply because we have come to the conclusion that the present economic system under which we are living is not capable of maintaining itself and at the same time taking care of the people. I think we shall have to face this fact in the near future. I know that when I make a statement of that kind many people think that I am simply ranting. When I cite the evils of the capitalistic system they say, no doubt, that I am simply taking advantage of an opportunity to voice a little cheap socialism. But we have reached the stage of the world's development where we have to face great economic facts; and even though some of the remedies may not be quite to the liking of some of those who in the past have advocated the present system and benefited by it, I submit that if such people want to maintain that system-I will put it on that ground for the moment-they will have to take some action of this kind. You can blow up a balloon to a certain limit, but if you blow it up too far, as we used to do as children, we know what the result will be. The balloon
bursts. Now I suggest that the balloon is pretty nearly at the bursting point, and if you really want to maintain the system as it is to-day I suggest that you let out a little of the air in the form of some relief to some of the people; otherwise there is apt to be a catastrophe. The balloon is apt to burst. I do not think that this danger can be simply swept aside as chimerical. If one looks at the financial system to-day, at the enormous dividends on which we are expected to pay interest, watered stock, and all that sort of thing, taxation and the international debt responsibilities we have, I think it must come home to every thoughtful member of the house that we cannot stand a great deal more, unless indeed the system is considerably more elastic than most of us imagine.
It would seem to me that we have almost reached the point where we shall have to face the issue frankly. To which are we going to give priority? Dividends, profits, vested interests of all kinds, or, on the other hand, the needs of men, women and children? There are those who say it is quite possible to pay large dividends and high wages. There are some who say it is quite possible to maintain our banking reserves and at the same time take care of unemployment. Well, I would suggest that now is an excellent time to try it out. I doubt very much whether it can be done. The overhead has become so great that we cannot very well carry that overhead and at the same time look after immediate needs. If you say we can, then we agree at least on this: You look after the immediate needs in the meantime, with the idea that it may be one way of perpetuating the system, and I will look after those needs with the idea that this is only the beginning of a break up of the system, being convinced that human needs ought to come before so-called property rights.
Going into various municipalities and in my own city. I find on every occasion that it is taken for granted that the bond interest is the first claim, and that if you cannot pay bond interest there is no use talking about helping unemployment. I may be heretical; you may call me bolshevist or whatever you like; but I say that earing for the needs of men, women and children in the community ought to have precedence over bond interest. We shall have to face that sooner or later, and in that connection I am tempted to say this. When we remember that most of the bonded indebtedness was incurred at a time when the buying power of the dollar was approximately twice what it is to-day, I would say that in all justice you should at least cut the bonded indebtedness in two in order to

Unemployment-Mr. Woodsworth
give. even the most fundamental justice to those who have to pay the taxes to pay the bonds. There is the situation as we have it to-day, and in this house we have that alternative presented to us. We come to vote estimates and I find a considerable amount which has to be paid by the government on account of our public debts; or the amounts to be paid are statutory, and that settles it. If it is statutory it goes through without even consideration by the house; it goes through as a matter of course. And immediately we are told, "Well, we cannot provide for any of these fancy schemes, in relation to unemployment for instance; we cannot provide for unemployment relief or insurance because we have not revenue enough to go around." And the bugbear is held up, that we shall have to pay greater taxation, of which we are all afraid. There is enough wealth in this country to enable us to stand a great deal more taxation, if that taxation were upon the great corporations and were not levied, as it is today, upon the rank and file of the small people of the country. So long as there is wealth which is being invested in foreign countries by people who have made it in this country, I say there are sources from which we can obtain greater funds. So long as we in this country are allowing the greater part of the wealth to pass down to the next generation, there are sources from which we can obtain increased taxation. After all, it seems to me that we have to get behind these financial questions to the real fundamentals.
We have enough wheat in this country to feed the people; we have enough timber to build all the houses; we have enough clothing to clothe all the people. At the moment I cannot think oLa single commodity produced in this country of which we have not a sufficient supply to-day. There is no use telling our people to go out and work harder; we should tell them, from an economic standpoint, that they should work a fewer number of hours per day. There is no use telling our people we should lay up more goods on the warehouse shelves when the fact is that we should enable them, in some way, to get the goods off those shelves. The fact, as recognized by every economist today, is that the question now is not one of production but one of distribution, but most of us are still living in the earlier pioneer days when we had to produce more as the only way in which we could eat anything at all.
We are living in an. age of surpluses; the question is not to get more but to distribute what we have. The unemployment we have to-day is a result of the labour saving devices which have been introduced during the last

few years and the labour saving organization that has taken place, which together have resulted in greater efficiency. Unemployment has resulted from these causes, yet we turn around and treat the poor unemployed almost as if they were criminals. If we, as a community at large, have in any way benefited by all this wonderful development of the past hundred years it seems to me that the very least we can do is to care for those individuals who through the maladjustments of our system are thrown out of work.
I would ask the government and the Prime Minister to give the most serious consideration to this question, and I would point out again that if there was any occasion to call a special session in September to deal with this question, there is an equal or greater oocasion for dealing with it at this stage of the present session.

Mr Speaker, I had intended to speak on the address, and had listed this question of unemployment as one of the matters which I wished to take up, but I am glad to take advantage of the occasion and present my remarks to the house now. This was the one policy amongst all the policies of the government on which I felt compelled to unhesitatingly and unqualifiedly criticize the government, the lack of any mention in the speech from the throne of any preparation for meeting the unemployment situation not in the past but in the future. I admit that if you look at the speech from the throne with a microscope you will find a very delicate reference to it, but a very cautious reference indeed. I find that the reference is to suggested
.... possible safeguards against a recurrence of the present subordination to world forces.
That is a very mild way to refer to the unemployment situation. The other references to unemployment in the speech from the throne all deal with the past, as to what has been done and with what success those measures have met. The speech contains nothing whatever to give us any hope or any anticipation that the government intend to bring forward at this session any proposals to deal with what is immediately, or very soon will be, in front of us. I refer to the destitution which will be in evidence next winter.
I believe that next winter the unemployment situation will be worse than it was last year, and I have several reasons for making that statement. The reserves are all gone. The workingman, the small man who had

Unemployment-Mr. Neill
put aside a little sum of money in order to allow his daughter to go to normal school to become a teacher, or to help his son go to technical school, has had to use that sum of money in the support of the family. The car has been sold, and so on. Then again, the municipalities, and especially the smaller ones, are in the same position. They thought they had an unusual condition to contend with last winter and stretched their resources. They spent money when they had to perhaps borrow it in order to help the situation. They were compelled to do so or they would not have received the assistance of the government in unemployment relief. These municipalities will not be in a position to do the same thing next winter. Even the railways will not be able to help as they have last winter. The big railway companies have been subsidized by the government, at enormous expense, to anticipate their building programs. They can hardly be expected to project their developments so much further ahead in order to do the same thing again this coming winter.
We find that other bodies take a similar view of this matter. I have in my hand a column out of the Vancouver Daily Province dealing with conditions in that city. A special meeting of the city council was called to consider this question of the conditions which will prevail next winter, and one of the prominent aldermen said:
But we must have concrete proposals for next winter, and not just drift along.
I am afraid we are just drifting along here, and will continue to do so until a desperate situation faces us. Then we find, as one of the hon. members who preceded me said, a reference to a small riot that took place last week in Vancouver. There were over 1,500 unemployed men engaged in that riot, in the middle of spring when there should not have been any person out of work. God knows how many more unemployed men were not engaged in that demonstration. In the same paper we find that a delegation went down from Nanaimo to Victoria asking the government what they were going to do to relieve the situation in that coal mining area, which is very bad at the present time. Again, in the last paper I reecived from home I find that Premier Tolmie is coming down here-and this may be news to the Prime Minister- to ask that $100,000 be given to the city of Vancouver to help out their present unemployment situation without the city being asked to match it dollar for dollar, because the city frankly state they have followed that policy up until now, but that the civic funds for relief purposes are virtually exhausted.
What are they to do unless Premier Tolmie can get that $100,000, and not on the basis of dollar for dollar?
As I say, now is the time for us to make preparations for next fall and next winter. We do not want to have to call a special session of parliament to deal with the situation, so now is the time for us to consider what plans can be made to meet the inevitable destitution that will ensue next year. I saw the case of the unemployed summarized in a couplet the other day, and with the permission of the house I will place it on Hansard. It was as follows:
Five wolves hunt for the soul of men
And all have hunted me.
Hunger and cold and fell disease,
Aloneness, misery.
I think that puts the situation in a sentence. I might go further than that and say, "Let us beware lest we allow these wolves to be turned loose on society." They have tasted blood, so to speak, in the sufferings of the unemployed, the destitute unemployed and their wives and children, but suppose they are not satisfied and want more. What a feast they would have if they were turned loose on the leaders of society, the big magnates of business, these people who feel secure in their wealth and position, some of them fortified by having it handed down for a generation or two. These people have acquired a sort of smug, contented outlook on life; they have really come to believe that they are of finer clay than the common run of humanity, and they think that no matter what suffering may come to the submerged masses, as the saying is, it never can come to them. I would suggest, however, that they be not too sure, because what has happened in the past may happen again in the future. We admire the massive bulwarks of the great concrete dam, which holds back waters which have a potential energy of a million horse power. But dams have been known to crumble and the greater the dam the more disastrous its deathdealing capacity, the more terrible the on-rushing force of the water which overwhelms the whole community.
In our day and generation it is not good to permit dry matches and powder to be too close together. It has been said that the cause of the French revolution was a remark made by a gentleman of high rank to the effect that if the common people were starving they could eat grass. Of course, that is quite wrong because a silly remark by an ignorant man was not the cause, but only the match which set fire to the powder, which was the realization by the people of the great chasm existing between what were called the upper
Unemployment-Mr. Irvine

and the lower strata of society; the litter lack on the part of the ruling classes of comprehension of, let alone sympathy with, the misery and degradation suffered by the masses of the people. The result was that the dam burst, and out rushed the pent-up forces of these desperate people, just like the water, careless of where it went, striking recklessly and wildly, doing great harm in the manner perhaps least calculated to produce the needed reforms of which the people themselves were only imperfectly aware. So, Mr. Speaker, I might warn the wealthy, ruling classes.
Where are they?

We should take steps now, not to prepare against a revolution but to prevent the causes of revolution. An hon. member asks: Where are the wealthy ruling classes? They are to be found in almost every country of the world in spite of our supposed democratic systems of government. If you doubt it, Mr. Speaker, obtain Bradstreet's report on the financial resources of the federal cabinet ministers. Or, if you like, do the same thing with reference to the cabinet ministers of the province of British Columbia. If that does not satisfy Your Honour, go to the big moneyed companies of Canada and inquire if they do not expect something in return for their large campaign fund contributions. Were those contributions made simply from a love of humanity? I rather doubt it.
It behooves us to consider how we can meet this situation or overcome these conditions. Remedies will have to be adopted and policies considered which are of a far-reaching character. Greater cooperation than that which now exists will have to come about between capital and labour. To-day some of the farsighted industrialists of the United States are looking towards that greater cooperation. I will not use the expression, "production for use and not for profit" because that would hurt the sensibilities of some hon. gentlemen opposite, but perhaps some of the best ideas conveyed in that phrase will sooner or later have to be adopted in our economic system. However, that is for the years to come, and in order to meet the situation which we will have to face for the next ten years there should be some form of unemployment insurance. As the hon. member for Winnipeg said, that cannot be brought about in a day because it would necessarily take time and be a contributory scheme which would have to be worked out by the best actuarial ability we have. The only thing we can do meantime is to make some provision for the emergency which is confronting us and provide work for the coming winter. That would mean the 
voting of money and the laying out of a program possibly somewhat similar to that carried out at the special session.
Let me conclude my remarks with a quotation from a hymn. I will mention that this is taken from the hymn book of the United church, because otherwise it might be thought that I was lending myself to communistic or bolshevik propaganda. This hymn is as follows :	.
When wait Thou save the people,
Oh, God of mercy, when;
The people, Lord, the people,
Not crowns and thrones but men.
Lord save the people, Thine they are,
Thy children like Thine angels fair.
From want, oppression and despair God save the people.

Mr. Speaker, the matter which has been brought to the attention of the house by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) is one of great importance to every hon. member of this house and to the country as a whole, but I regret very much that it should have come up in the manner in which it has. The government and the house being very anxious to get certain business completed, I shall occupy only five minutes of the time of the house. This subject is of such importance that I could not sit quiet without taking part in the debate.
I desire to suggest what to me seems to be the practical thing to be done under the circumstances. If the distress in the country is as great as hon. members have represented it to be, there is no doubt that the government will have to take similar action to that taken last year. There is no doubt that had that action not been taken conditions to-day, bad as they are, would have been worse. It will be necessary to dip into the treasury and spend some money if present conditions continue and I suggest the following, not as a solution for unemployment, but as a practical proposition for immediate relief. The farmers are in need of relief. The hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) is asking that certain definite relief be granted for agriculture, and the government may have to do that. My suggestion is that the government purchase so many thousands of bushels of wheat, the eggs that are now rotting without a market, as well as the meat impossible of purchase by hundreds of thousands, and establish in every city a distributing food centre for those out of employment. That would settle the grub-stake of those people and with the same money would provide a certain amount of relief to the farmer.

Unemployment-Mr. Heenan
I would suggest also that the government build highways and undertake other public works as quickly as possible so as to create employment. In order to do this, the government should issue treasury notes which could be taxed back again when times improved. Times will become better; we will have another of those funny things they call cycles no matter which government is in power, and then these notes can be taxed back and no increase will be incurred in the national debt. Those are my suggestions and I will not stop to develop them. I am sure that the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is listening, as well as the hon. ministers on the front benches, and probably they will do something about it. Hon. members who have spoken during this debate have spent too much of their time in discussing fundamental problems without considering the matter of immediate relief. I hope if any more speak they will be more specific as to what should be done after to-morrow when the relief will be withdrawn.

Mr. Speaker, when a similar debate took place at the last regular session I recall that I was criticized by the then opposition, now the members of the government, for having allowed so many speakers sitting on the opposition benches to discuss this important question without my making a reply on behalf of the government. Several hon. members of the apposition have urged today that something be done for the relief of unemployment, and yet not one member of the government has risen to state the case of the government. At that time I had to confess that although I was vitally interested in the question of unemployment, I had not suggested and could not suggest a cure for it; but the present government, during the last campaign, assumed the responsibility of ending unemployment. Therefore if the members for the Winnipeg constituencies and the hon. member for Vancouver South, the three Labour members, urge upon the government of the day to do something towards relieving unemployment, the responsibility is one which the government has taken upon itself. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) when speaking at Regina on June 10 last, as reported in the Leader-Post of June 11, had this to say, referring to the government of the day:
They play with the lives of men and women. What for? Do they realize there are lives that they are playing with, food for wives and children, hunger? Nine years of wasted effort before the great betrayal. It did not take Judas that long.
Again, speaking at Regina on the same day, as reported in the Toronto Globe of June 11, he said:	[DOT]
When you gamble with a nation's prosperity for power the result is inevitable. The government of to-day has not seen the to-morrow,'- they have only thought of to-day and thinking only of it the result has been that now we have unemployment, people walking our streets, men and women hungry,-we have all these things in this great rich country.
Again, speaking at Moncton on July 10 last, the present Prime Minister had this to say:
The Conservative party is going to find work for all who are willing to work, or perish in the attempt. It is going to call parliament at the earliest possible date after July 28 and take such steps as will end this tragic condition of unemployment and bring prosperity to the country as a whole. . . . Mr. King promises consideration of the problem of unemployment.
I promise to end unemployment. Which plan do you like best?
Again, speaking at Quebec, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of July 14 last, the present Prime Minister said:
There was no necessity for a conference on unemployment, he continued. The solution was too apparent. "What you want is work," he exclaimed, "not conferences, and you are going to get work." Unless his promises to the people of Canada were kept if elected to office, Mr. Bennett said he wanted Quebec and other members of his party to vote him out of office.
There are other promises along those lines, but I am not going to take up the time of the house in quoting them.
