In view of these statements it seems strange that not one word with respect to how the government proposes to end unemployment is contained in the speech from the throne. It was not surprising, therefore, .that the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) should inquire a few days ago as to what the government proposed to do with respect to the relief of unemployment. I am sure every hon. member W,as astonished that the government made no answer to his question. Under the circumstances it was the duty of the hon. member for North Winnipeg to bring the question before the house in the only way that I suppose he could do so. It was also surprising to find that instead of inviting suggestions from the opposition or from members sitting behind the government, members of the government rose in their place m order to endeavour to prevent a discussion from taking place. I consider it is the duty of the government to make a statement to the house and to the country as to how they propose to end unemployment.
There is no question that the unemployment situation is far worse than it was when
Unemployment-Mr. Heenan

the Prime Minuister made those promises to the people. One has only to take the figures supplied us over the signature of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) as of March 1. Hon. members will find that when my hon. friends took office in August last, the index of employment reported by over 7,000 firms in Canada stood at 118.8, and that a decrease occurred every succeeding month until on March 1 it stood at 100.2, or more than 18 per cent fewer employed in those industries than when my hon. friend took office. That is a confession of failure. I do not know what opportunity my hon. friends from Quebec and other districts who are sitting behind the government are going to take advantage of in order to do as the Prime Minister invited them at Quebec to do, namely, vote him out of office. But while they are considering that matter, we might point out that under the measures brought down during the special session, the government appropriated $20,000,000 for the relief of unemployment and made contributions to the municipalities and the provinces, with great beating of drums and blowing of trumpets, but they actually withheld public works for which appropriations had been made by the preceding Liberal government and which would have employed workmen throughout the country. According to the report of the Department of Labour, work amounting to 3,975,355 days' work was supplied to 228,355 men, an average of sixteen days' work per man from the time the act went into force until the first of March. Under what conditions? The conditions hetT out in the regulations and under which the grant was made to the provinces and the municipalities, provided that the prevailing rate of wages should be paid to the workingmen, and that the same working conditions should apply. Nevertheless we have in northern Ontario, of which I am most conversant, men working to-day at starvation wages, not at prevailing rates that obtain in the district, and under such conditions that if they open their mouths for a minute they are deprived even of the pittance they are receiving.
What are the railway companies paying for the same class of labour?	[DOT]
Forty-three cents an hour for the lowest paid men they have. Doe3 the hon. member want me to show him the contract indicating what the men are receiving ?
I do not think the exMinister of Labour is correct in that.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to be interrupted. One of the ministers of the Ontario government, after I spoke at Hamilton, stated that in northern Ontario they were paying the same rate of wages that obtained on the railroad. I have in my office a schedule of wages and working conditions showing that the wages of the sectionmen on the railway run from forty-one to forty-three cents an hour.
I am talking about the extra gangs.
Why does the hon. member not raise the question as to what they are paying in Russia instead of looking for the lowest wages in Canada?
We are talking of conditions in Canada.

I have in my hand a
schedule showing the prevailing rate of wages in northern Ontario. When I had the honour to be Minister of Labour, we had public buildings under construction in northern Ontario and we had officers who went out and secured figures showing the prevailing rates of wages, according to the Labour Gazette for December, 1930, the prevailing rate of wages paid on the public building at Keewatm was 42-J cents an hour for common labour and 50 cents an hour for skilled labour. In the same territory, an Indian public school was being erected at Kenora, and the rate of wages paid on that building for common labour was 42i cents an hour, as reported in the Labour Gazette for February, 1929. On a public building at Fort Frances, according to the Labour Gazette for October 1929, common labour was paid 40 cents an hour and skilled labour 50 cents an hour. The Labour Gazette for August, 1930, reports that on a public wharf at Kenora common labour was paid 42i cents an hour.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are the prevailing rates of wages in my district, and yet in spite of the agreement that was made between this government and the government of Ontario, the provincial government is denying to its labourers a proper scale of wages as provided for in that agreement. I was very glad to hear the Acting Minister of Labour in this house (Mr. Gordon) say in reply to a question I put to him the other day that if any provincial government or other body was not pp.ying the prevailing rate of wages the federal grant would be withheld until the wage rate

Unemployment-Mr. Pouliot
was adjusted. I thank my hon. friend for saying that; it is what I expected him to say.
I would point out to the minister that it really means the holding back of thousands and thousands of dollars of which the workingmen of this country have been robbed up to the present time, and in that connection I would suggest that as there have been three million working days up to the present, and I am satisfied that in many instances as much as one dollar a day has been withheld from these men, say three million dollars, a royal commission should be appointed in order to see that these men get justice. I know the conditions that prevail all through northern Ontario, and I know that if any of these men had complained that they were being deprived of this pittance, they would have felt the heavy hand of the Ontario government, acting for its own selfish ends. I do not intend to take up more of the time of the house; I think that we should have some answer from the government.
I could go on and advocate a policy of unemployment insurance. I am satisfied that if the government of the day will follow up what was done by the late administration, we shall have unemployment insurance in this country before very long. This house has already gone on record as endorsing the principle of a contributory system of unemployment insurance. The house did declare that under our constitution it was a matter coming under provincial jurisdiction, but declared further that the matter should be taken up with the provinces at the first Dominion-provincial conference. We were in touch with the provinces in connection with the matter before we left office. Some of the provinces have endorsed that principle. I noticed that only the other day the premier of Manitoba stated that that province was in favour of unemployment insurance and had conveyed its ideas to the Dominion government and asked for a conference, but as yet had not been advised as to any such conference. I consider that it is the duty of this government to state, not only to the hon. members from Winnipeg, but to the whole house, what they propose to do, not simply to end unemployment but to relieve immediately the present urgent conditions.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): I have a few remarks to make, Mr. Speaker, before the end of the fiscal year Yesterday I asked the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) if the items in the estimates that were not expended during the fiscal year lapsed to-night at twelve o'clock.
He said, yes. I am very glad to see my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) in his place. I am very sorry that the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) is not present, but I would ask the Prime Minister to ask the faithful messenger who brought down the Welland canal contract last night to 'look after the Minister of Marine this afternoon.
The Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways are both familiar with the question which I am about to bring before the house. I have already supplied them with all the facts relating to the non-building of the station at Riviere du Loup by the Canadian National Railway.
There was first a report by the director of the provincial board of health, dated December 21, 1928. It is in French, but I will read it for the benefit of my hon. friends who both understand the French language very well. It is addressed to the Acting Chief Commissioner of the railway commission, and reads:
Quebec, December 21, 1928. Mr. Thomas Vien, K.C.,
Acting Chairman,
Railway Commission,
Ottawa, Ont.
My Dear Mr. Vien:
Complying with my instructions, Doctor A. Barabe, medical officer of the Sanitary Unit of the county of Temiscouta, accompanied by Doctor Dumais, District Inspector of Health and Mr. Labelle, Inspector of the Unit, inspected the station of the National Railways, at Riviere-du-Loup.
I have just received their report and I deem it my strict duty to forward you a copy without further delay.
The perusal of this report will acquaint you with the unwholesome sanitary condition in which the Riviere-du-Loup's station is kept. This railway centre is the most important existing between Levis and Moncton, and 1 hardly can understand why the public place herein mentioned is so neglected.
On many occasions we notified the officials of the Canadian National Railway, from Sir Henry Thornton down to and including the Divisional Superintendent, of the deplorable condition, not to say unwholesome in many instances, of the station under the management of the Canadian National Railways, in our province, and invariably we received the answer "That they would look into the matter, that the lack of appropriation had prevented them, heretofore making improvements, that certain reports received by us were exaggerated, etc," with the result in the end that nothing or little is ever done to meet our claims.
In no way, do I wish to impute to anybody intentions or dispositions which he has not. but 1 wonder how it is having visited many places in this country, that in other provinces we see tidy stations where hygienic precautions exist, while in the province of Quebec, some stations are in a deplorable state.
I am verv sorry to trouble you, but in dealing with dilatory methods to which some have
Unemployment-Mr. Poidiot

recourse in order to evade our requests, I cannot do otherwise than calling your attention to this matter. I hope you will forgive me and trust that I shall not have to publish the report in question in order to obtain satisfaction.
The conditions prevailing in Riviere-du-Loup exist in numerous stations in the Lake St. John and Chicoutimi districts, and in many other stations under the Canadian National Railway system, and to which I have already drawn the attention of the official authorities.
I feel confident that in bringing to your notice the state of things of which I am complaining you will find means to help us in the best interests of the population which the National Railway system serves in our province.
Your obedient servant,
The Director,
Dr. A. Lessard.
The conclusion of the report is as follows:
After reading this report, it seems to us that the conclusions are easy enough to draw. Tho fault lies in the condition of the building which is very old, and poorly kept. Adequate repairs would be difficult to carry out and with perhaps doubtful results.
Without being taxed with exaggeration, we wish to state that only a new building would answer the purpose, if the officials of National Railways have at heart improving this station to the satisfaction of the travelling public.

the date?

I have not the date, but I may say to my hon. friend that it was sent by Doctor Lessard at the same time as the letter of December 21, 1928, to Mr. Thomas Vien, Railway Commissioner.
Last year during the special session, Mr. Speaker, I brought the attention of this government to the fact that before any further money for unemployment was spent the appropriations which had been made during the regular session of 1930 ought to be exhausted. Of the amounts allocated to the use of the Canadian National railways nearly $80,000 was put aside for the building of a new station at Riviere du Loup. That station, one of the oldest in the province of Quebec, was built by the old Grand Trunk Railway Company. The Canadian National Railways decided that it was time to build a new station. After conditions were explained to the railways and shipping committee, the money was voted by the house, but since this government took office nothing has been done. Money was voted for the improvement of the wharf at Riviere du Loup, but, on account of some strange circumstances which I explained to the Minister of Public Works the other day, only part of it was spent. There was money for the building of a post office at Trois Pistoles. The sum of $20,000 was set aside for that purpose, but nothing was spent.

Money was set aside for improving the wharves at different places, but only a portion of that money was spent as a measure of unemployment relief.
A resolution was passed by the chamber of commerce of Riviere du Loup on April 19,
1929,	asking for the building of a new station. Also on April 22, 1929, a resolution was passed by the town council of Riviere du Loup to the same effect. On May 1, 1929, the general manager of the Atlantic region of the Canadian National railways, Mr. Appleton, wrote as follows:
May 1, 1929.
Louis S. Pornmet, Esq.,
Secretary,
Chamber of Commerce,
Riviere du Loup, P.Q.
Dear Sir,-This will acknowledge receipt of your communication of the 22nd ultimo, enclosing copy of resolution passed at a meeting of the council of the Chamber of Commerce of Riviere du Loup, held on Friday, the 19th day of April, 1929, respecting Canadian National Railways station building at Riviere du Loup and would advise that this matter is receiving our earnest attention and the necessary arrangements are being made to include an item in our budget for 1930 covering the construction of a new station building and appurtenances, for the consideration of our executive officers.
Yours truly,
(Signed) W. U. Appleton,
General Manager.
The deputy minister of railways wrote me thus on Maj' 10, 1930:
In answer to your letter of May 5. I wish to advise that there has been included in the Canadian National Railways budget for 1930 an item of $77,136 for the construction of a new station at Riviere du Loup, P.Q.
This detail is taken care of by section (d)
of vote number 323, 1930-31 estimates.___
Yours faithfully,
Y. I. Smart,
Deputy Minister.
The total amount voted was $52,870,000. The amount necessary for the building of a station would be only a small sum as compared with the large sum I have mentioned. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that there has been no pressure brought to bear by politicians in connection with the building of this station. The matter was pressed upon the railway commission by the board of health, and following that the Canadian National Railways took action by putting an item in their budget for the building of the station. On May 28,
1930,	Mr. L. V. Hummel, principal assistant to the president of the Canadian National Railways, wrote me thus:
Dear Mr. Pouliot:
In reply to yours of May 19, I beg to advise that plans are now being prepared for a new station at Riviere du Loup.

Unemployment-Mr. Pouliot
As soon as these plans are ready, it is the intention to call for tenders, and have the work done by contract. In view of the size of the building, it is impracticable for us to construct the station with our regular B. and B. forces.
Yours faithfully,
L. V. Hummel.
On July 14, 1930, Mr. I. C. Rand, general counsel of the Atlantic region of the Canadian National Railways, wrote thus to the city of Riviere du Loup:
We are anxious that the work be proceeded with without undue delay.
He was speaking on behalf of the Canadian National Railways. I have in my hand a poster published by the Conservative candidate. This poster is full of promises and in section (e) of article 6 the promise is made to build the new station so long expected at Riviere du Loup. This poster was published on July 24, four days before the election.
I now come to the words used by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. During the campaign my right hon. friend spoke at Brandon, the constituency of the former Minister of Railways. What did the present Prime Minister say upon that occasion? In the Winnipeg Evening Tribune of June 23, 1930, I find the following:
Again declaring his opposition to an amalgamation of -Canadian Pacific and Canadian National Railways, Mr. Bennett said he had just heard a new canard to the effect that if elected he would appoint one of the Canadian Pacific Railway officers to the presidency of the Canadian National. "Can you imagine anything so ridiculous?" he asked. "I want to say that the Conservatives in power will give the Canadian National management a stronger support and a more disinterested support than they have had under the King administration. There will be less log rolling and interference. The management will be better able to carry out their policies without politicians butting in and trying to stop them.
On August 22 the hon. Minister of Railways wrote to the perpetual Conservative candidate in my constituency. That gentleman stated that he was independent from our leader and from Mr. Meighen, when he supported Mr. Patenaude. Later he became a partisan of Mr. Meighen and afterwards of the right hon. the Prime Minister. I hope his fidelity to the latter party will last long.
He polled a big vote.

Yes, but since then some
of the people who voted for him have been operated on for cataracts. The hon. the Minister of Railways wrote to that gentleman. The information I have in my hand is in the French language, but with your permission Mr. Speaker, I will translate it.
I have received your favour of August 20, with enclosures. 1 shall be pleased to do all I can with regard to your proposals or suggestions.
I believe I am properly quoting my hon. friend.
On September 19, during the short session, I asked concerning the prices submitted by each tenderer for the work on the Riviere du Loup station. The reply was that it was not in the interest of the public or the railway to divulge any information of this character. Then I asked two further questions:	What
tender was accepted, and on what day; and on whose recommendation would this work immediately be carried out. The answer was that no tender had been accepted and the matter was under consideration. That was several weeks after the tenders had been received in Moncton. I am told that those tenders reached Moncton on August 26. The government were then studying the matter very carefully; I believe they were thinking about it. On October 3 my hon. friend the Minister of Railways was on his way to Hudson bay. He was replaced by the acting minister, the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley), who was sworn as such on October 7. I am sure the Prime Minister will admit that the hon. member for Argenteuil was sworn in as acting Minister of Railways in order to put into effect the policy of this government to take a million and a half dollars from the unemployment relief fund in order to pay the interest on the proposed work of the railways, amounting to $21,000,000. That is the reason why the hon member for Argenteuil was appointed acting Minister of Railways. The Prime Minister is in the house and he will not deny it.

The point is this, that his colleague the acting Minister of Railways, the hon. member for Argenteuil, was appointed temporarily to that office in order to carry into effect the policy of the government to take $1,500,000 from the unemployment fund in

Well, I am dumbfounded if the Prime Minister does not know anything about it. I would ask the Minister of Railways whether it is not a fact that the reason the hon. gentleman was appointed acting Minister of Railways at the time was as I have stated.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I presume he was appointed to act as Minister of Railways for all purposes. What the hon, member mentions is only one of them. The government dealt with it.
Was he appointed acting Minister of Railways in order to refuse to sanction the construction work at Riviere du Loup?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Certainly not.

I am very glad to hear my hon. friend say he was not, but as a matter of fact it was the first thing the acting minister did, because he was sworn in on October 7 and his first act was to send a wire to the Canadian National Railways informing them that he had refused to sanction the building of that station.
Yesterday I read two telegrams and I asked my hon. friend who had recommended to the acting minister that he refuse to sanction the carrying out of that work. He did not answer me, but he said that the cost involved was the reason why the station had not yet been built. The decision was arrived at under instructions from the acting minister, because -the Prime Minister is enough of a business man not to allow any department to be carried on without one of his colleagues in charge when the minister of that department is away from the capital. October 7 was the very day the newspapers announced that the Canadian National Railways were starting this program of construction throughout Canada from ocean to ocean. I have many clippings here, but I will not quote them now; I have not the time at present.
There is another point which I wish to mention. It was understood that there would be no politics in connection with the unemployment fund, and this is the presumed intention of the order in council of Friday, September 26. There was some correspondence between the Board of Railway Commissioners and the railways, who said that the repairs mentioned by my hon. friend in the telegram which I read to the house yester-

day were sufficient. But they said something further, insulting to my constituency. In a letter dated January 23, 1931, Mr. Alistair Fraser makes this statement:
The floor area is slightly over one-third of the area of the whole building and is ample to take care of all purposes.
There is no cellar in that building, it is falling to pieces; but it is good enough for the people of Temiscouata county.
I have another communication, a report from the medical officer, which was forwarded by him to the secretary of the railway commission on January 30, 1931, by the director of the provincial board of health:
Dear Sir,
I deem it my duty to forward to you the enclosed further report of the Sanitary Medical Unit Officer of the county of Temiscouata with reference to the unhealthy state of the station, at Riviere-du-Loup.
As you will observe on reading this document, a building of such importance should have a cellar of equal dimension. As regards the sewer system, it is certainly defective and of a nature to be noxious.
It would be desirable that your Commission make the necessary representation in this matter with the Canadian National Railways.
My time is limited and therefore I will not read the report just now; I will read it tonight on the railway estimates. I brought the matter to the attention of the Minister of Railways, to whom I despatched the following telegram on February 25, 1931:
May I draw your attention to my letters of 16th and 23rd instant. As proposed repairs to Riviere du Loup station do not include construction of basement therein hot improvement tst ?ewer system nor repairs to foundation. U ill you sanction same as satisfactory although condemned by board of health? If you do not approve proposed repairs will you reconsider decision regarding immediate construction of new station building?
The reply was this:
Your telegram received in absence of honourable Dr. Manion. Minister acknowledged your letter 23rd before he left city yesterday.
F. T. Collins,
Private Secretary.
No further answer came. There is another letter from the assistant general counsel Alistair Fraser, dated March 3, 1931, in which the following statement is made:
In stations it is not customary to construct basements the entire area of the building, and the basement area is generally confined to a size suitable for the requirements of the heating apparatus and coal bin.
This is the policy of the Canadian National Railways. Now let me read to the house this excerpt from the Montreal Gazette of February 25, 1931:

Unemployment-Mr. Pouliot
W. W. Atterbury, president of the Pennsylvania railroad, announces that the company's $175,000,000 improvement program, which includes the erection of new stations, will cover a period of two and a half years. In the United States, as in Canada, it is evident that the railways have great faith in the future. They are giving tangible proofs of this and are furnishing extra employment when it is most needed.
Mr. Atterbury, as everyone knows, was the mentor of Sir Henry Thornton, in his younger days.
Now, Mr. Speaker, to sum up the matter. First of all, the board of health condemned that station as unhealthy and recommended the building of a new station; and the chamber of commerce-and city council of Riviere riu Loup, supporting the report, passed a resolution which they sent to the railway officials. Moreover, the general manager of the Atlantic region declared that it was important to build a new station at Riviere du Loup. And as a matter of fact the Canadian National Railways included in their budget, without any undue interference on the part of politicians, an item from that building. The Conservative candidate promised that that station would be built as soon as my right hon. friend came into power. And now, first of all, he asks the minister not to take any decision in the matter until he comes to Ottawa. That must be so, because the railway was anxious to have the station built. But we find that no action was taken on the tenders for the reason that all expenditures on railway capital, and otherwise, have to be approved by the minister. But this course would be followed in any case, as the minister knows. I say that in the first place there was interference in the fact that the Department of Railways did not go on with the matter, as it should have done, in accordance with the views of the Canadian National Railways.
A resolution was passed by the city council of Riviere du Loup on November 3, 1930. It is quite lengthy and if my hon. friends wish to have it I will read it on the railway estimates to-night. But my hon. friend the ether day said that the Conservative candidate had been working as hard as I have done for the building of the station. Why have I worked hard for it? First of all, because I am proud of my constituency. I believe such a shameful building as the present one is a disgrace to the community, and all thought that last winter, when times were so bad, would be the proper time to have a new building constructed.
My hon. friend the minister was fair to me in saying that I have been working very 22110-314
hard for that station. That is true, and I thank him for that remark, but he was very unfair in stating that the Conservative candidate has been working just as hard. The hon. gentleman himself has written to the contrary to the city council of Riviere du Loup. In a letter dated November 6, 1930, to the secretary-treasurer of the city of Riviere du Loup, he said:
Votre cite ne fut pas proposee d'une maniere speciale lorsque la question fut posee.
The translation is: "Your city was not proposed in a special manner when the matter came up." How did the matter come up? On October 7 the Department of Railways and Canals and the Department of Labour were joining together to give millions of dollars to the railways in order to allow them to spend a great deal of money to relieve unemployment. At that very time the Conservative candidate and his assistant were in this city. They did not go to see the Acting Minister of Railways, the hon. member for Argenteuil; they could not see the Minister of Railways, because he was on his trip to Hudson bay. They did not even see the acting minister, who perhaps has been exiled in disgrace to Buenos Aires because he stopped the building of the station at Riviere du Loup. The acting minister wrote the Conservative candidate and said, "You certainly did not come to see me during the past six months, nor have I had the pleasure of meeting you since the election last summer." If that gentleman worked so hard for the station how was it, when he came to Ottawa on October 7, Christmas Day for the unemployed, that he did not even go to see Santa Claus in the Department of Railways and Canals? Perhaps that was the reason why the right hon. Prime Minister chose one of the oldest members of the cabinet to represent Santa Claus, who was to give so many gifts to the people in order to help them. What has happened to bring about this discrimination against my constituency?

speechtext: May I interject a few words in an attempt to clear the air? When this matter was decided by the Acting Minister of Railways and Canals, the minister himself was not in Ottawa, neither was the Prime Minister or the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre), who has spoken along somewhat the same lines. That is why I have been indulgent so far with the hon. minister, but I will now inform him that he should speak only of things whereof he knows.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals

When I make a statement it can be proved. I speak the truth. What about what my hon. friend said in Toronto in December, 1927:-"I believe the Conservative party has been too honest in the past. Our party in the past has been too honest in strictly defending its position and policies on controversial and sectional questions." The Liberal party has been honest in the past and will be honest in the future, and that is the difference between the Liberal and Conservative parties.
I have been courteous enough to give two minutes, or one fifth of the remainder of my time, to my hon. friend, and I desire to proceed with my argument. My hon. friend

has stated that the two travellers have been working to have this station completed, but he knows that that is not ithe case.

If the hon. gentleman does not know it, then he should not speak.

Can my hon. friend speak of things about which he has no knowledge? Did he have a special channel of communication with his department, which was kept open while he was on his way to Fort Churchill?
Mr, MANION: The hon. gentleman called on me a number of times and discussed this matter; that is how I know.

Before the Tory candidate knew the amount of the tenders he still expected that his partisan protege or partner would secure the contract and thus benefit both of them to the prejudice of the people in my constituency. Then when my hon. friend found that he could not satisfy the greedy appetites of his Tory friends in my constituency, the population as a whole were forced to suffer.
I have a high regard for the Prime Minister and he knows it. I have high respect for the Minister of Railways and will continue to hold that feeling so long as he does not repeat the erroneous utterances made by the Tory candidate in my constituency.
The Canadian National Railways intended to build this station at Riviere du Loup; the money was voted by parliament, but the elections came along and when the minister was asked to hold up this matter he did so. The department has refused to sanction the building of this station, which is a direct interference with the decision of the railway officials. It is " log-rolling and butting in " of the worst kind. The department was told: " If you cannot give this contract to my protege who submitted one of the highest tenders, do not give it to anyone else." The people were made to suffer because that man could not obtain the contract. I will say this to the right hon. the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways: I have no desire to cause them any inconvenience, but I want to know what is going on. I promise them that if I do not receive a satisfactory answer I will demand an explanation for every dollar in the Canadian National Railways estimates. Those estimates will not pass before the com-

Unemployment-Mr. Denis
ing recess if that explanation is not given to the house. If such action is taken in connection with $100,000, what would be done with $13,000,000?
I believe the Prime Minister was sincere when he expressed such lofty ideals at Brandon. I trust that he will stand by those ideals, and that is one reason why I have attempted to let him know what is going on within the ranks of his party in order that he may have an opportunity of putting a stop to these practices.

Mr. Speaker, I am quite pleased that the unemployment problem was debated, in the house, from the very outset of the session, because it is precisely the one to which our good Conservative friends resorted most during the last campaign in order to win the election. Since the very beginning of the session, I have closely followed all the very interesting speeches which were delivered in the house. However, I wondered why the hon. ministers of the crown seemed to neglect this matter. Seldom have ministers so persistently absented themselves from the house as has been done since the beginning of this session. They could certainly profit by the nice things we have said and show some gratitude for the good advices we offer them, with all due courtesy and consideration so as not to wound their susceptibilities.
Up to the present, only one or two of them have been bold enough to rise in their seats in order to uphold their policy. I well understand their bashfulness, considering the numerous pledges that they and their friends made during the last election campaign. They had to face a situation which, instead of improving became considerably worse, and, having no excuse to offer for their inability to remedy the ills which they pledged themselves to cure should they assume power, they preferred to remain silent. It is now, sir, eight months since the present government took over the administration of this country. Have we witnessed any change in the economic crisis under which we have been suffering for more than a year? Is unemployment still with us? Have our workers been able to get work to provide for themselves and their families? Have the farmers of the province of Quebec and other provinces found more remunerative markets for their products? Did the Prime Minister, while in England, find markets to facilitate the wheat sales of the western farmers who are grievously suffering because of this handicap.
I can positively state, sir, that the present government has done nothing to relieve the
economic depression which we are undergoing. It was nevertheless a pledge given during the last election campaign: In three days it was to relieve unemployment. The latter still exists, even to a greater extent than in July, 1930. The government failed to carry out its pledges. However, to be fair to our friends on your right, sir, I must admit that there is one pledge they carried out: that of having parliament meet immediately after the elections. The session took place in September last, at this emergency session the government had an amount of $20,000,000 voted to relieve unemployment, and thereby give work to our working classes. It was a splendid deed, and I shall not deny, sir, that the impression created among our distressed workers, was one of satisfaction. It is now more than six months since we voted that amount and I find, in a report published lately, that Quebec heretofore, received, out of the total amount, but $155,414, this includes $36,455 which was given as direct aid.
I wonder, sir, whether the act was of great assistance to the 30,000, or more, unemployed that we had during the winter, in Montreal? Can the government boast of having in any way relieved unemployment? I think, sir, that this legislation-like all their election pledges-was designed to lure the Canadian people.
The hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) feels quite hurt when we charge the government with not having fulfilled its pledges and shown incompetence by not putting an end immediately to unemployment which existed and still exists in this country; a crisis which they were to relieve in three days. On the contrary this crisis is, to-day, more acute. Our workers, in Montreal, are unemployed and I can state that the satisfaction which they felt in September last, has entirely disappeared. They are unanimous in stating that the government deceived them and are not worthy of the trust placed in them. In no way do I wish to put the blame on the Quebec government or the municipal administration of Montreal, but I state that from September to the beginning of this month no work has been carried out to relieve the unemployed. How are we to explain this delay? I, for one, find no other reason than the red tape to which were subjected our provincial government and municipalities previous to receiving the grants. I think, sir, if the present government had been sincere in having those $20,000,000 voted, a sum which was to give the unemployed a ray of happiness and prosperity, they could have handed over this sum to those interested in a more expeditious way, so as to have it distributed during the
Unemployment.-Mr. Denis

winter. No doubt the law had to take its course. For the time being, I do not object, provided however, that all the provinces be treated on an equal basis. That is not what happened and I intend to prove this fact immediately. In their eagerness to help Ontario-the latter having nearly always shown sympathy for the Tory policy-the present government authorized an expenditure of $2,000,000 over and above the amount allotted to her from the $20,000,000 appropriated by parliament, in September last, for the relief of unemployment. And this was done without any other authority than that of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion), who told the contractors:
Owing to the unemployment crisis, you may oarry on the work, I grant you $2,000,000 more. The province or the municipalities will not be called upon to contribute their share in carrying out this work.
What became of the authority of parliament? They scoffed at it, ignored it. To-day, in their meek way the government asks parliament to legalize an act the purport of whioh is to favour Ontario to the detriment of all the rate-payers of this country. I state again, it is always the same Tory policy, "favouring their friends."
Just think, only one job has been started in Montreal out of the grant voted to the unemployed-I mean the tunnel of St. Hubert street, under the Canadian Pacific Railway. Nothing else heretofore has been started. There is of course a shovelful of earth which was dumped into a small pail by a member of the Executive Committee of Montreal, at the Wellington street tunnel, under the Lachine canal, this is kept as a souvenir of this wonderful feat. Moreover the work has since stopped owing to some difficulty which arose between the Department of Railway and Canals and the city of Montreal. If this can be called a remedy to unemployment, then I state, on behalf of the numerous workers of St. Denis riding who suffered extremely from the crisis, that you have not lived up to your pledge and responsibilities, and I charge you with having failed to carry out your duty. You are too incompetent to remain at the head of the administration of this country. You now come and beg of us to give you an extension of time. Our answer is: what you were unable to carry out in eight months, you will not be able to accomplish in a year or more. Your policy rests on absolutely false economic principles. The high tariff changes adopted in the course of the emergency session have not resulted in the benefits hoped for. Quite the contrary the working classes which form the larger part of the consumers FMr. Denis.]
are still obliged to pay for the necessities of life, prices which are not in keeping with their wages. Worse than that, your high protective tariff, sir, has been profitable but to one class of people: the large financial and industrial interests. You have deprived the working class of the benefit of this fair and legitimate competition that we, the Liberals, were happy to grant through a moderate tariff, and which was detrimental to nobody. Both consumers and producers were fairly and equitably dealth with. That is why, Sir, that under the late administration, union and harmony always existed between capital and labour. Our country witnessed happy and prosperous days; now, I fear that under the present regime depression will increase and that the worst calamities are yet to come.
Eight months of administration, is too short a time to relieve unemployment! Yet, it is long enough to increase the public debt by more than $100,000,000, and too brief a time to find markets for the sale of our western wheat. Did not the Prime Minister, as well as his friends, state, that if the people sent them to the Imperial conference, they would force England to purchase our wheat? Did they not state that if dynamite were needed, they would make use of it to blast their way to success? The Imperial conference took place. The Prime Minister, together with some of his ministers were delegated to attend this conference, and they also returned but disconcerted and downhearted. No markets were found for our wheat.
The British government looked upon the proposals made as absurd, and they discovered that a Bennett was not a King or a Lapointe, and still less a Laurier. The government hide themselves under the mantle of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and try to impress on the people the idea that the proposals made in London by the Prime Minister were about the same as those made by our great leader in 1902 and 1907, at the conferences which he attended. Sir Wilfrid Laurier asked that a preference be given to colonial products, leaving, however, Great Britain free to grant it or not. He did not ask Great Britain to tax her food products so as to favour those of Canada. This, however, was done by the right hon. Prime Minister. Laurier would never have been so bold as to proclaim "Canada First" at a conference where all the delegates from the various dominions were convened to discuss the interests of the whole empire.
It is the first time that a Canadian Prime Minister made such a blunder, and I hope it will be the last time. Canada on that score

tJnem ploy men t-M r. Denis
was subjected to the worst humiliation. I am amazed, sir, that the members of the cabinet do not realize the great blunder which the Prime Minister of Canada made. I heard, the other day, the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) apologize, saying: " After all, the proposal of the leader of the government was not bo bad as our opponents contend, since all the delegates of the Dominion gave him their support." Did the hon. Postmaster General take the trouble to study and does he realize what is the total amount of business each Dominon does with Great Britain? Is he aware that Canada alone among the British dominions has a favourable trade balance- and does not this fact give him some matter to ponder over? If we sell to England for nearly $100,000,000 more than we purchase from her, is the Prime Minister jutified in stating: "Canada First"? It might, perhaps, have befitted the other dominions to express such a thought, exactly for the reason just given, as England was justified in her reply to the right hon. Prime Minister, "England First".	,
There is to be another conference this year. No doubt, the Prime Minister, profiting by past experience and remembering his "flop in England, will not be guilty of the same sin. This will be in the best interests of Canadians. No doubt, he will carry out the policy which has been followed up to the present by the Liberal party, and which gave such excellent results. In order to derive the best possible benefit from this conference, I think that the remarks of the Postmaster General should now find their application: "Should not the interests of the country, especially in the present crisis, have precedence over party interests?" The country needs markets to sell its surplus products; home markets are inadequate as an outlet for its products, and in order to engross such markets, we should avoid surrounding ourselves with a prohibitive high tariff, so as to prevent foreign products from reaching us. How do you expect to sell without purchasing from any one? That is, however, the exact policy followed by the present government, and it has been the cause of our export trade decreasing by nearly 894,000,000. Carry on, gentlemen, things are coming your way! In four years, our country will have lost its place of honour among the trading nations of the world to return to the rank of an inferior nation.
I hear it said by our friends on your right, sir, that since they are in power a great change has taken place in trade and industry. How wonderful they are! They have no fear of ridicule! But truth tells a different story.
Everything is tottering! Everywhere threats,
brawls and revolutions appear. Only last Saturday, over 2 000 unemployed tried to enter the city hall at Montreal, to ask for work. They were prevented by the city police. Being unsuccessful, they marched to the Champ de Mars where speeches were made, begging the authorities to put an end to their hardships and privations by giving them work. The working classes are tired of waiting. Again last week, in Montreal, hundreds and hundreds of workers invaded the municipal work-yards. They were seeking work but could not secure any.
This is, sir, the situation as it exists to-day. Not only in Montreal but throughout the country. Is the government aware of this? How can they find an excuse for delaying repair work to the extent of $1,500,009-amount appropriated by the late government -repairs which were to be carried out to the Wharf of the Pointe-du-Moulin-a-vent? Our unemployed would have been much relieved by such work during the cold winter days, bread and butter would have been thankfully received. The government cared not, the fate of the poor people seems indifferent to them. They preferred to delay this work because the lowest tenderer was not a favourite of theirs. The crisis which we are passing through matters little to them. The hardships of the unemployed matters little to them; what matters to the Tory government is protection to their friends. Let the country perish, providing that millions of dollars fill the pockets of their friends! The same old Conservative and Tory policy. People of Canada, my country, my cherished land, you must bear up, be patient. You are at the beginning of your hardships and troubles. Pray to God that He may enlighten the government in order that, at least, the evil done against our country be not irreparable.
Previous to resuming my seat, allow me, sir, to inform the hon. member for Jacques-Gartier (Mr. Laurin), and all those who think like him, that Quebec is not a Conservative province; it was so at one time, previous to 1S96, when education had not spread among the people. To-day, thanks to the education received, Quebec knows better, it has become Liberal, and it will remain such.

That is why
the Conservatives carried off 24 ridings.

Your hopes are but wild dreams. You are in the opposition at Quebec and you will remain there for a long time, in order that justice and liberty may always reign in our province and the rights of minorities be respected. Harmony exists
4S8

Unemployment-Mr. Rheaume
among all the races which make up its population. May its example be followed by the other provinces of confederation.
The recent events which have taken place in Saskatchewan-among others the disallowance of French in public schools-are not of a nature to cement harmony and union which should exist among us, and such means will not help in making a great and prosperous people in this country. Let us resolve to cease our appeals to race and religious prejudices. Let us be fair and generous in everything and everywhere. We shall thus end by understanding and knowing one another better. It is -by concerted action that our country will more quickly and easily reach its noble destinies.

Mr. Speaker, I owe it to my constituents to apprise you that I represent the finest riding of the province of Quebec and of Canada, because, since confederation, it has always remained loyal to the Liberal party-this is evidence of the foresight; and enlightened patriotism on the part of the true Canadians of both sexes whom I am privileged to represent in the house.
My riding is both agricultural and industrial. The farmers carry on mixed farming and endeavour to improve their flocks. They have always been satisfied with the policy of the Liberal party and they understand that in a world-wide crisis the farming class may suffer like other classes in the community.
I listened closely to the speech delivered by my neighbour, the hon. -member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel) who contended that the trade conventions of Canada with Australia and New Zealand were detrimental to the Canadian farmer. The farmers of his riding like those of my own carry on mixed farming. They therefore meet with the same conditions.
Last September, sir, we were called to attend an emergency session in order to vote $20,000,000 and thus settle the question of unemployment; that is, to fulfil pledges made by our opponents during the election. In answer to my hon. friend, the member for Missisquoi, who stated the other day, in the house that the city of Farnham, which is located in his riding, had recently made great progress, I 'have a letter here which reads as follows:
Farnham, Que., March 21, 1931.
Mr. Martial Rheaume, M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir:-
With reference to our conversation by telephone, this afternoon, I wish to inform you that two new factories were established here in 1929, about the month of March: one the 
Collins & Aikman Company Limited, manufacturers of plush, etc., and the other the Dewey <fc Almy Company Limited, manufacturers of chemical products. In 1930, as I had recently the opportunity to inform you Barry & Staines Linoleum (of Canada) Limited, established themselves here, also about the month of March, 1930.
J. E. Lefebvre,
Secretary-Treasurer,
Town of Farnham, Que.
No other factory has since been established I must point out, sir, if the town of Farnham has progressed, if these factories were established there, it is due to the Liberal policy. I may add, if my hon. friend the member for Missisquoi is among us to-night, he owes his mandate to the pledges he gave during the last election. This gentleman with his friends went from door to door telling every farmer who had lost cattle as a result of the tuber-culine test, that he was authorized 'by his leader, Mr. Bennett, to promise $20 -for each animal killed within the last three years. I know farmers in that riding that have lost as many as 30 head. It was certainly an alluring offer.
As to the question of unemployment, I wish to state that in St. John we have an industry which employed, in 1929 and 1930, 1,400 people. Since September 2, 1930, to January, 1931, this factory worked 32 hours iper week, and since then 24 hours per week; in the week ending March 21, 1931, 42 persons were dismissed. There only -remains at present about 900 people working at this factory. I ask my friends the Conservatives where is to be found their success in relieving unemployment? The hon. member for Jacques-Ga-rtier (Mr. Laurin) stated the other day that the government had fulfilled all their pledges; that he himself had obtained the construction of two tunnels; I do not intend to -further discuss this subject because my hon. friend the member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis) discussed it at length.
I do not wish, sir, to miss the opportunity of answering a remark m-ade a short while ago by the hon. member -for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Dorion); he stated that the Conservatives had carried off 24 ridings in Quebec. I think, sir, that the hon. member for Quebec-Mo-nt-morency-I do not know what pledges he made -to his constituents-^must have taken his cue from the other Conservative candidates of Quebec. I cannot resume my seat without answering a remark -made by the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve), member for Laval-Two Mountains, who in his speech on Thursday last, rebuked the Liberals for not having made any suggestion. I think, sir, if the hon. Postmaster General had remained in his seat from the very outset of this debate on the address, he would certainly have heard

Unemployment-Mr. Maclnnis
suggestions made 'by members on this side. He was conspicuous by his absence. I well remember that last year he taunted the exmember for Laval-Two Mountains for having been indifferent to the debates in this house. The hon. Postmaster General at present seems to exhibit the same failing. I think that this indifference at times applies to him.
I also recall the pledges of the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) the member for Chambly-Veroheres-my neighbour-during the last election. I realize that his success in the election was somewhat of a surprise, like that of many Conservative members from Quebec.
I know that the hon. Minister of Marine made numerous pledges, especially to some of my personal friends whom he persuaded to vote for him because of the advantages and favours that he would grant them. Since parliament was convened I know of no bill introduced aiming at fulfilling the pledges that the Minister of Marine gave. He also promised an indemnity to the farmers who had lost cattle, owing to the tuberculine test; he promised that they would be paid at the rate of 82.50 per hundredweight; that their butter would sell at 45 cents per pound, and that the bridge between Longeuil and Montreal would be exempt of tolls. Conservative candidates throughout the country made numerous pledges to the electorate, however, if to-day new elections were held the result might perhaps not be the same.
I do not wish to delay the house any further;
I only wanted to take this opportunity of expressing my views. In the course of this debate on the return of prosperity in this country, the hon. members on your right, sir, censured us and at times these gentlemen told us: "Do give us a chance." A few days ago I had the privilege of listening to the speech of the hon. Postmaster General. I am not aware that he has prepared any program, he who always proclaimed himself, when in Quebec, 'the champion of the farming class. I think that he will take 'his cue from his leader whose policy is rather to favour manufacturers and industrialists.

I should like to say a few words in
connection with the question raised by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). Probably like many other members representing an urban constituency, I have received during the last few days many letters and resolutions from various organizations in reference to unemployment in the part of the country from which I come. Sharing a room in this building with my hon. friend from North Winnipeg I took these resolutions to him in the hope that out of
his wealth of experience he could tell me what should be done. He told me that he would move the adjournment of the house to bring the question before it. I asked him what support he expected to get. "Well," he said, "last year we had the whole Conservative party with us." "That looks very good," I said, "because there are a whole lot more of them in the house this year, so we ought to make quite a showing." But to my painful surprise, when the question was raised this afternoon it met with the active opposition of the Conservative party, who were so sympathetic when the same question came up last year, and that notwithstanding the fact that the situation at the present moment is worse than it was on the 31st of March last year. In my innocence I could not understand what had caused such a change. Is it possible that to move from one side of the house to the other can change men's minds so radically, although the outward circumstances have not changed in the slightest, in any event not for the better? When the house is not sitting I intend to sit for a few moments on the other side just to note the psychological effect.
That is the only way you will ever get here.

Perhaps, but you may
get over here.
In discussing this question, Mr. Speaker, I shall not approach it in a critical spirit It should be dealt with, I think, from at least four points of view. We should consider, first of all, the extent and the seriousness of the present conditions; secondly, what steps should be taken to meet the present pressing situation; thirdly, desirability of a full investigation of the causes of unemployment and of the economic depression; and lastly, what permanent steps may be taken to meet the situation generally and provide against these ever-recurring periods of depression.
Touching first on the seriousness of the situation, I am continuously in touch with my own city of Vancouver. Although perhaps there are not so many unemployed there now as a month ago, the number is very much greater than it was a year ago. Not only that, but the city's resources to meet the situation are not nearly so great as they were a year ago A deputation from the city of Vancouver met the cabinet of the local government at Victoria on the 23rd of March last. The chairman of the relief com-mitee pointed out to the government at that time that the city could not meet any funds that the government might have left

Unemployment-Mr. Maclnnis
over from the appropriation voted last September, and therefore the making of provision for the unemployed at Vancouver was up to the provincial government. On the same day a deputation waited on the city council to arrange for the reinstatement of 1,500 single men who had been cut off from relief under the act. On March 18, just a few days ago, 6,064 married men were securing unemployment relief. In view of a situation of that kind I think it rather strange that we have not heard a word from the government side of the house as to their intentions in connection with unemployment.
My hon. friend from North Winnipeg pointed out at the beginning of his remarks to-day that he had referred to this question about a year ago. May I quote a few words from Hansard of April 2, credited to the present Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) He said:
Mi Speaker, I agree "with the hon. member who introduced this resolution that it is the most important problem facing our country to-day.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if the subject of unemployment was an important problem facing our country in the year 1930, when the situation was not as bad as it is to-day, when the financial resources of the municipalities were not depleted to the extent they are to-day, and when the financial resources of the people themselves were not depleted to such an extent, how much more serious must that problem be now? Yet we do not hear a word from the Minister of Railways and Canals.

We are not as wise
as the monkeys.
Mr. MaeINNIS: I quite agree that we are not as wise as the monkeys, in this particular at any rate. I suppose we think we have progressed very considerably since our savage ancestors roamed the forests, but if it were possible to bring one of those ancestors back to the world now, where he could see the hungry, cold, unemployed, with all this wealth at our disposal, he would rightly think we have not progressed so far after all. I continue quoting from this newspaper:
Instead of cooperating men separate themselves into groups. They build walls round these groups and sometimes one group will go mad and begin to throw stones at another. They have not yet learned to regard the earth as belonging to their whole race in common; they have not discovered how to organize themselves-their nations, their classes, their sects are not less quarrelsome and hardly less foolish than the gulls or the tomtits, which are very foolish little birds!
I think that is along the lines of cooperation which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has been advocating in this house for many years, and surely it is time we began to have that cooperation in view

Unemployment-Mr. Maclnnis
of the fact that our efforts along other lines of endeavour have failed to assure the great majority of people in this country any decent share of the wealth which we are producing in abundance.
What is the reason for all this? The hon. member for Queens (Mr. Myers)-and I refer to this partly because Prince Edward Island happens to be my native land-stated the other day that no one seemed to know *what was the cause of unemployment. 1 have been wondering whether no one does know, or whether possibly some people do know and do not like to state the cause for fear of hurting somebody's feelings. I believe I know the cause, and in order that my hon. friend from Queens may go away from this house a little wiser than he came I am going to tell him, whether he believes me or not. The cause of unemployment is private ownership of the means of production. That is the one and only cause. Hon. gentlemen may ask for the proof of that statement, and I will give it. Let us suppose all the people in the world were gathered together in this room.
T admit that it would be quite a dreary place in which to live, but for the sake of argument let us suppose all the people in the world were gathered together here and that we owned everything in common. Could you imagine one of us going cold or hungry while we had all this wealth at our command? But supposing Mr. Speaker or someone else owned all the wealth, and the rest of us could have access to it only whenever he wished to let us do so whenever we paid tribute to him for doing so. You could well imagine our going hungry and cold in circumstances of that kind. That is the only cause of unemployment, and it will not be remedied until the machinery for wealth production is socialized and put in the hands of the people to be used for the common good.
Hon. members may think this is a wild statement to make, but we are not alone in that opinion. I hold in my hand a resolution which was passed at the regular session of the Alberta conference of the United Church of Canada, held in McDougall United Church, Edmonton. According to the Parliamentary Guide this is the church to which my right hon. friend the Prime Minister belongs, and for that reason if for no other he should give some consideration ito the resolution, which states:
Whilst we endorse and approve the Remit, in that it states certain items of advancement and improvements in reference to industrial conditions, and the increasing recognition of
human rights, yet we are convinced that such a statement is inadequate for the present time, and that the church should express itself in terms other than those which simply endorse principles that have for some years been ger-erally appreciated, even though the principles involved have not thus far become fully operative;
We believe that, in harmony with the teachings of Jesus, we should proceed as rapidly as may be possible to the creation of an order based on cooperation and service, which would displace the present competitive, acquisitive social order.
That is not my statement; it is the statement of the Alberta conference of the United Church. The resolution continues;
In the centre of the thinking of Jesus was man and his need, as a contrast up to the present the essential feature of the economic system is profit.
That is what we have been contending for years; that is what the hon. member for North Winnipeg and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre have been telling this house for several sessions. The resolution continues:
The present system has now been under trial for a sufficient period of time to lend itself to fair criticism, and the present unhappy condition of over-production, under consumption, unemployment, and attendant uncertainties, is its condemnation.
We certainly never used words any harsher than those in connection with the system under which we live.
We are convinced that in the Father's world there is a sufficient abundance of necessary commodities to meet the needs of His children. The demand of the day is to bring these commodities under Christian control and distribution, a result which finance under private control as the connecting link between production and consumption has failed to secure.
In the meantime, we advocate such methods as unemployment insurance, contributory old age pensions, along with a program looking forward to social control of the means of production, distribution and exchange.
We have never advocated more than that; we have never asked anything more than recognition of the fact that under the present system the more we produce the less secure is the position of the individual. All we are asking is that means be taken to change the system as quickly as possible to one that will give us a standard of living according to our ability and wilingness to work and produce. Just imagine the amount of wealth Ithat could be produced with modern machinery by the 300,000 unemployed who are walking the streets of this Dominion to-day, if they could only have access to the means of life. Just imagine it, and tell me whalt it would mean. Why cannot we have access to these means of life? As I said before, the reason is

Unemployment-Mr. Maclnnis
because these means are in private hands and we cannot get to them without paying tribute to some private person. There may be half a dozen or probably less than a hundred people in this Dominion who exact tribute from all the rest of the people for everything they eat or wear and for every move they make. The resolution continues:
We believe that society should regard enforced unemployment as an intolerable menace, producing an unemployable class with slum conditions, wastage of human energy and personality, and threatening war or revolution. We believe that governments should grapple with the problem with energy similar to what would be used in a national emergency.
I do not believe that the members of the government are alive to the present situation. We have similar conditions in every city, town and country district in the Dominion. The following is a portion of a letter I received from a gentleman residing near Saskatoon :
There is no money wherewith to pay taxes, store bills, interest on loans, etc., and the people in the north, while having produce from gardens, etc., to live on have not any money wherewith to buy clothing. One school teacher has asked for clothing for 57 children; another for 40; another for 34 and another for 16. Children cannot attend school because they have nothing but last summer's cotton underwear and canvas shoes to wear.
I think the suggestion made this afternoon by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) would help us considerably. Much more could be said as to why we are faced with these conditions and why we cannot expect any improvement in the near future.
I have here some statistics given by Sir John Aird at the annual meeting of the bank of Commerce held in Montreal, as follows:
From the period between 1926 and 1928 the population increased by two per cent, food production increased by 8 per cent and the production of raw materials by 11 per cent.
The people are much worse off in 1929 and 1980 than they were in 1928, although there was an increase of eight per cent in the production of food and 11 per cent in the production of raw materials as against an increase of two per cenit in population. We should have some explanation from hon. gentlemen who pretend to run the government of this country.
In conclusion, I beg leave to move-

Order.

So far as the Annuities
Act is concerned, this amount is required to liquidate liabilities already incurred for the advertising of annuities and the payment to representatives and postmasters of commissions and allowances earned in getting business for which the appropriation in the main estimates was inadequate. A question was asked as to the change in advertising. The present administration continued until January of this year, the plan which had been carried out by the former administration. At the end of that month the contract with McConnell & Fergusson Limited was terminated. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There was appropriated in the main estimates the sum of $30,000; by governor general's warrant $50,000 was provided, and this estimate provides for an additional sum to make a total of $95,000 in all. The total expenditures up to March 27 amounted to $77,938. There was the Amalgamated Builders Council prosecution, which absorbed $25,784. There was the motion picture inquiry, which absorbed about $20,000; the bread inquiry; and sundry items to be made up by this estimate. There were the expenses incurred in connection with the payment of counsel for the case which went 'to the privy council determining the validity of the Combines Act. The bread inquiry accounted for $1,728.15. The total includes a sum not contemplated last year when the estimates were passed, necessitating a further sum being obtained for the purposes mentioned.

The other day I asked the Prime Minister a question. Probably the fact that I did not give notice of my question resulted in the Prime Minister not doing himself justice in his answer. I referred to a combine which according to reports is to be consummated within a few days, involving about $690,000,000 invested in the pulp and paper industries of Canada. The report went on to say that if this combine took place high priced mills would be closed and low priced mills would be kept open. As my right hon. friend knows, the Combines Investigation Act is more often used to prevent injury to the public than to remedy a grievance after the occasion for it has arisen. I was wondering if the Prime Minister would think it advisable to make some kind of inquiry to learn whether or not this combine is likely to injure the public interest. I am sure my right hon. friend will realize that if this combine is allowed to take place and results in high priced mills being closed down and low priced mills being allowed to operate, the effect will be detrimental to the towns and villages which have been established in the vicinity of these so-called high priced mills. If the combine is likely to injure the public generally, and especially the people in Quebec and northern Ontario, there should be some interference by the government.

Supply-Pensions

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did endeavour to explain to the house, as I do now to the committee, that the question of the jurisdiction of this parliament in the matter would certainly be a controversial one. The authority of parliament concerning the application of the Combines Investigation Act in such a case could not be antecedently determined; whether or not a combine exists is a matter to be determined after the combine forms. At the present moment no such combine as that described by my hon. friend exists. If a company were incorporated in which these enterprises to which my hon. friend refers were merged, I hold grave doubt as to whether the Combines Investigation Act would apply to such a company. That certainly has not been determined. So far as the court decisions go, such a condition would not amount to a combine within the statutes. So far as property and civil rights are concerned, the closing of mills and dealing with property and questions of that sort can be determined by the provinces in which the crown lands are situate and from Which the timber is taken. If it be private timber the same observation applies, except in the case of the province of Manitoba where crown lands were leased to private enterprises. If such lands have been transferred to the crown in the right of the province of Manitoba they are subject to the laws of that province rather than the laws of the Dominion. I repeat that the question whether or not a combine exists is a matter which can be determined only from the facts of the case as they arise, and not antecedently. I assume no company would be created which would contravene the laws of the Dominion.
