Also a letter from Mr. Meehan, of Toronto, acknowledging receipt of a letter sent by the minister with regard to the matter. These are the communications.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will my right hon. friend place them on the table?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. I was going to
give them to my right hon. friend.

I rise not to object to item
51 but rather to ask the Minister of Pensions and National Health-if he may be allowed to answer, because he has borne the brunt of the attack in connection with this matter- for an explanation as to why this relief to pensioned soldiers, from an emergency relief fund granted by this parliament, was cut off without a word of warning, and restored only when such a strong protest of public opinion swept the country, the pressure of which not even this government could withstand. Why were the soldier organizations throughout the country not consulted before this step was taken? It has been stated-and I should like an explanation as to this-that the cut was made in order to effect economy in the administration.
We have heard a good deal to-day with respect to the unemployment question. We know that for the ordinary unemployed the emergency relief measure did not expire until to-day, and it does seem to be due to the returned men of the country, and to the people of Canada as a whole, that some explanation should be given as to why, without a word of warning, the pensions of these men, whose very existence was dependent upon this relief, were cut by the Minister of Pensions and National Health.
I would also ask the returned veterans in the cabinet to give an explanation, because there are some veterans here in the cabinet before me. The hon. the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sutherland), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir), the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion), and the Minister of Pensions and National Health
Supply-Pensions

(Mr. MacLaren) are all returned veterans. 1 have here a statement given out to the press by the Mail and Empire as follows:
In justice to the other war veterans in the cabinet it can be said they were not aware of Dr. MacLaren's proposal and it is doubtful if any of the other ministers were consulted.
I am going to ask the Minister of Agriculture whether he was consulted in this matter. Did he consent to the pensions of these returned men being cut? If he, was consulted what did he do in the matter? I pause now for an answer. His silence apparently would imply that he was consulted and is not going to say what he said. I will ask the Minister of National Defence: was he consulted by the Minister of Pensions and National Health, and if so, what did he say with respect to the cutting off of these pensions to returned men? Is he not going to be allowed to answer either? I would ask the Minister of Railways, who apparently is the only one in the cabinet who has been allowed so far to speak: was he consulted by the Minister of Pensions in the matter of having these pensions cut at the time they were? Was he consulted? If so, what opinion did he give in that regard? AH I can say, then, is that it does seem strange to me that parliament should be witnessing the spectacle of members of this government, three or four of them returned veterans, remaining in their places and not offering any explanation to the house with respect to this matter. I have nothing but the kindliest feelings towards the Minister of Pensions and National Health. I believe he has the interest of the returned veterans at heart, and I believe it was his desire, to do justice to them. I should like also to have an explanation as to why; although that minister-bore the brunt of the attack, when it came to restoring the order, the right hon. the Prime Minister attempted to take all the glory, boldly announcing the pension would be restored. In fact there was no glory about it; he was merely performing a duty which should have rested upon the Minister of Pensions. I say, Mr. Chairman, that the country awaits some explanation-*
Oh, oh.

This is not a laughing matter. For the benefit of some who may be ignoiant of exactly what this pension meant, may I say that the relief allowance was granted only to pensioned soldiers. These soldiers whose pensions were not adequate to meet their needs were granted something extra in order to carry them through the winter. Single men were granted $30 per month and the allowance was graded from that amount up to 
some $67, but whatever pension they were receiving was deducted from that amount, so you will see that these men were receiving barely enough to allow them to exist. This is what the Minister of Pensions cut, and I want the country to know that that is exactly what was done by this cabinet in order to effect an economy. That is where they began.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: May I inform the committee that the amount was never cut? Perhaps if the hon. gentleman had been a little more careful of his facts he v'ould not have fallen into the error of making the statements he has made. He must have known that no pensioner ever received a lesser sum than the sum which is now being paid and which was paid at the time.
I beg the right hon. gentleman's pardon; I never suggested it was cut or that a pensioner received anything less, but the order went through cutting these amounts from coast to coast.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No order went through; no order was made.

Then why did the right hon.
gentleman say he had restored it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There was a misapprehension on the part of those who, like the hon. gentleman, conceived that what they saw in the press wras an authentic statement of what had happened. It was not. What happened was very simple, and I should like to explain it to the hon. gentleman. This is not something out of which political capital can be made. In 1928-29 there was an appropriation of $250,000, and there was $378,987.86 expended. Last year $550,000 was voted and only $517,000, in round figures, was spent. This year we originally voted $250,000, and in November of last year $275,000 in addition was obtained by governor general's warrant. I assume it is known to hon. gentlemen in this committee that to obtain a governor general's warrant there must be urgent necessity. The minister obtained the $275,000 in November, and in February of this year $225,000 further was sought. It was represented that the urgency was not sufficient to warrant the payment of the sums that had been paid and it was suggested that a smaller sum would meet the necessities of the case.
The provisions with respect to relief are as follows: Relief may only be granted to a pensioner provided the amount of pension which he receives on his ow'n behalf and that of his dependents, combined with earnings or other family income, is not in excess of the maximum rate issuable in his particular

Supply-Pensions
category. Where the need of assistance has been established the combined income may be augmented by the issue of relief orders to the maximum rates set out. They are as follows:	Single men, $30 per month; man
and wife, $45 per month; man, wife and one child, $57 per month; man, wife and two or more children, $67 per month. It was believed by officers in the department concerned that the payment of the smaller sum would meet the situation at that season of the year, and for some reason it was represented in the press that an order had been made accord-ingiy.
As the hon. gentleman knows, no such order was ever made, nor were any payments at the reduced rate ever provided by the department. The minister obtained a further governor general's warrant for the $225,000, and on March 6 of this year an additional governor general's warrant was obtained for $75,000, making a total of $825,000. To maintain the payments up to date will require an additional sum of $90,000. Up to the date of the meeting of parliament on March 12 of this year, expenditures had been authorized which would amount to approximately $901,000 in all, and the additional sum required will carry it on until midnight to-night, as I have said. I may say further, for the information of the committee, that the number receiving aid increased very considerably this year over last year, hence the anxiety of the minister to be certain that there was the urgency for the warrant which I have mentioned. During the fiscal year ending March 31, 1929, the number of times relief was issued was 36,002; the number of men who received relief was 4,647; those eligible for disability pension numbered 50,620. For the year ending March 31 last the number of men eligible for disability pension had increased to 57,044, and at the present moment the number stands at 65.332. The number of men who received relief increased, up to March 31 of last year, to 5,548, and this year to 8,222, and the number of times relief was issued increased to 51,000 for the year ending March 31, 1930, and to 79,380 for this year.
It was under those circumstances the relief was granted, and the reason the statement was made by myself rather than by the minister was because a delegation waited upon me, and they asked that the statement be made in the terms in which it was made, because there had been no change nor had the minister contemplated a change unless the circumstances warranted its being made.

I am not quite sure that
the right hon. gentleman has stated the facts
as they became known to the public through the press.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is another thing.

Perhaps the right hon.
gentleman would permit me to discuss the matter for a moment. My recollection is that a statement was given out by the officers of the department to the various branches throughout the country, to the effect that after a certain date the payments under the unemployment relief provision would be reduced. No sooner was that statement issued than telegrams began to pour into Ottawa. I am quite sure the right hon. gentleman will not say these telegrams were based on nothing, or on vague rumours. They came from such important men as the president of the Canadian Legion at Winnipeg, or perhaps it would be the president of the Army and Navy Veterans' Association. He stated:
Winnipeg branch. Canadian Legion, in general meeting, protest very strongly action of Department of Pensions in reducing allowances to pensioners at this season of year.
He had been advised by someone in the department-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend should
not add those words "in the department", because I received just such a telegram as that and at once sent back a reply that no such action, so far as I knew, had been taken by the department, and I am informed that no such action was taken.

I am quite willing to admit that the statement of my right hon. friend is quite correct, but it so happened that I came to Ottawa at just about that time and a statement was issued either by the department or by the. minister himself to the effect that there were no longer any funds available. That appears to be borne out by the fact that the governor general's warrant was issued about that time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is right.

The statement was that there were no longer any moneys available and consequently a reduction would have to be made. I have not before me the statement made by the minister but I can easily obtain it by sending to the library for copies of the press of that day. I do not think the Minister of Pensions and National Health will deny that he made such a statement to the press in which he said there were no longer any moneys available and that the matter would be discussed by the, cabinet. Am I right in making that statement? The right hon. gentleman apparently nods, so I take it he nods in acquiescence.
Supply-Pensions

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I read it in the paper.
Do I take it that the right hon. gentleman says he read a statement purporting to emanate from the Minister of Pensions and National Health?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I read in the morning press, I think it was in both papers, the statement to which the hon. member has referred and I was advised by the minister that it did not interpret correctly the remarks he had made.

I find now that the hon. minister, who apparently cannot speak in this house for himself, can speak to the newspapers and be misinterpreted. Apparently this is becoming a habit of the government, and it is one which should be corrected. I suggest that the schoolmaster upon all occasions when his ministers speak-they will not speak in this house-be. given a copy of their statements in order that he may correct them, cross all the t's and dot the i's. Otherwise similar mistakes will occur.
The right hon. gentleman admits that a statement purporting to emanate from the Minister of Pensions and National Health was issued to the press. He claims that the press misinterpreted that statement, but surely the minister himself could have contradicted it. However, one or two days went by and then the Prime Minister said: These moneys will continue to be paid. Would it not have been possible during that time for the minister to have made a statement to the people of this country, to the ex-soldiers, that he had no idea of refusing payment, and that his statement had been misunderstood? I feel sure that if Hie. minister had felt that his statement had been misinterpreted or that an incorrect version had been given of it, he would have been the first to tell the newspaper men of their mistake. He is a man possessing broad sympathetic views, he has a kindly heart and is particularly well disposed toward the soldiers of this country, and he should have been the last to permit himself to be misinterpreted in this way. I think if I ask him now to tell the country and this committee whether or not he issued a statement which could be understood to mean that the relief to pensioners was to be reduced in some degree, he will answer. If he does I promise to take his word for it and I will not check him up even by reference to the newspapers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

I would like to follow up the statements made by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) by reading the statement issued to the press by the minister and asking him whether or not it correctly interprets what he intended to say. The following appeared in the Mail and Empire of February 18, 1931, under the name of a very reputable member of the press gallery, Mr. Blacklock:
To-day Dr. MacLaren said the reduction "is regarded as a somewhat temporary measure and it is hoped an improvement in the rates will be effected before long." The text of his statement reads:
"The issue of relief by the department of Pensions and National Health was always regarded as an emergency measure. It was never intended that it should constitute a permanent addition to pensions. The relief issue through this department is restricted entirely to pensioners."
"This year the demands have greatly exceeded the appropriation passed by parliament and much more. The number of applications for relief have more than doubled as compared with previous years. At January 31 last, the amount expended was something more than double the amount expended during a similar period last year."
"Complaints have been made as regards the distribution of this relief, and the relief has been placed on the minimum scale pending investigation. Consequently, the administrative officers of the department were informed that, pending further instructions, a reduction would be made in the amounts issued. This reduction is regarded as a somewhat temporary measure, and it is hoped that an improvement in these rates will be effecter before long."
"In no case will hardship result, for there will be such readjustment as will meet the circumstances."
I now ask the minister whether or not that correctly interprets the statement given to the press, and I plead with the Prime Minister to permit the minister to answer for himself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, one
would think it was more important that justice should foe done by voting this money which will enable payments to foe made, rather than to make political capital out of the need for the payments. Those of us who have listened to the speech of the hon. member for West Lamfoton (Mr. Gray) must be struck with the fact that it was a palpable effort to make political capital.

Mr. Chairman, I take serious
objection-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No one can have any
doubt as to that. It was couched in language which left no doubt as to its purpose. A

Supply-Pensions
statement was read in connection with which I stated a moment ago the minister could claim a wrong interpretation. The minister had no money and a governor general's warrant had not been issued. The law is that governor general's warrants are to be issued only in* urgent cases and that the money is to be treated as a trust fund. The language of the statute leaves no doubt as to its meaning, that at least a matter of necessity must arise. It is not a case of simply issuing a warrant when one feels like it, there must be occasion for it. The exact language with respect to governor general's warrants, must,
I fancy, be known to every hon. gentleman here who has had anything to do with the administration of affairs in this country. The money having been exhausted, it became necessary to issue a new warrant, and complaints were made that there had been aJbuse of the moneys that had been paid. The minister made that perfectly clear, and said that pending an investigation he proposed to carry them at a lower rate. This was construed as meaning that actual payments were to be made at a lower rate. I do not say that the statement was not open to that construction, but no such payments were ever made. The payments were continued because it was apparent from the statements received by the minister from every part of the country that a lower payment would not in any sense meet the demands of the situation. Therefore a governor general's warrant was at once issued and another one has been issued since. With the house in session, no warrant can now be issued, and if this sum is not voted, the payment cannot be made.
We are not opposing it; we are only asking for information.
We are not opposing the voting of this sum. We have a right to the information.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am endeavouring to supply all the information asked for. Before a governor general's warrant is issued, the minister must first satisfy himself that there [DOT]is not the ordinary, casual necessity for it, but the real necessity that warrants the substitution of the executive for parliament, [DOT]beause that is what a governor general's warrant means. In the exercise of that power the minister made inquiries and I think as the hon. member for Quebec South has said, very few days had elapsed. It may well be, as the hon. member for West Lambton has said, that the matter was hurried by
reason of the manifestations of disapproval. *No one doubts that, but the minister was seeking to ascertain exactly what the situation was, not to create a prolonged carryforward of the reduction of the amount to be paid, but to determine whether or not there was any warrant for the statements that had caused the investigation to be made, and whether or not the conditions were such as to entitle him to ask a further warrant as he did. He obtained it and payments were made as I have indicated.
Perhaps it is not quite fair to the house to suggest that members are not allowed to speak. I have undertaken the carriage of these estimates through the house and I shall endeavour to discharge that duty. When it is suggested that hon. members are not permitted to speak, of course that is entirely erroneous. No such relations exist between my colleagues and myself. We had an understanding, believing these estimates would be treated as estimates of this character for the period ending the current fiscal year would be treated. We believed the course followed in the past would probably be followed in this instance, and that they would be through in a few hours. We were disappointed in that regard; but having undertaken this duty, and having been supplied with the necessary information, I am endeavouring to carry it out in my capacity as Minister of Finance in charge of the supply bill. I am not complaining, but I do not think it is creditable to hon. gentlemen to suggest that any member of the administration is not permitted to speak. Any member of the house may freely express his opinion; but having undertaken to deal with these estimates, I shall continue to deal with them as long as the house permits me.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
As regards the concluding remarks of my right hon. friend, I may say that he can scarcely wonder that we on this side have the impression that members of the ministry have been forbidden to speak, since it has not been possible, with one exception, to secure a reply from a single minister of the crown with respect to any matter affecting his department. The Prime Minister may arrogate to himself the right to handle all the estimates, but to do so is not following British parliamentary procedure. It is not treating the House of Commons as it ought to be treated. It is not fair to his cabinet, and it is not fair to the country. He may say that his ministers are free to speak, but the impression the country is getting of the ministry is that it is composed of a number of nonentities.
Supply-Pensions

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The right hon.
gentleman was a nonentity last summer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am expressing the view that the country has of the ministers, in the light of what has taken place in the course of the discussion on these estimates. I do not say that hon. gentlemen are nonentities. I know some of the ministers very well and I know they are perfectly well able to take care of themselves in discussion. Moreover, I know many of them have a very wide parliamentary experience and might not only have contributed valuable information in the course of the discussions but have done much towards the proceedings of this house in having them conducted in the manner in which hon. members generally would have liked to see them conducted. I submit it is not treating the House of Commons as it should be treated, for the Prime Minister to take upon himself the work of the entire ministry in the House of Commons in connection with the explanation of matters affecting different departments. The Department of Pensions and National Health is one of the most important departments in the government. The war veterans throughout the country wish to hear what the minister in charge of that department has to say with respect to a matter which vitally affects them and their families, and they have a right to hear him. When the Prime Minister begins to lecture the opposition for assuming a certain attitude toward himself, he is entitled to know what the opposition thinks and what the country thinks. What we have been witnessing here looks more like procedure in a kindergarten than what is to be expected of the government of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Of course I do not intend to reply to language such as that. If the right hon. gentleman thinks that in so expressing himself an ex-prime minister is adding to the dignity of the House of Commons, I am content. This I will say: when he undertakes to speak for the country he seems to think he is still in power; he is not in power.

The Prime Minister seems to be very easily offended to-night, and I shall have to bring back again his wonderful smile.
I am much surprised that the Prime Minister takes exception to the word "kindergarten." It will be remembered that a former prime minister of Canada, the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden, who is still alive and is a distinguished man, at a lecture given in

Ottawa said that the League of Nations, which is an international institution, was just at the kindergarten stage, and no one was insulted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

I would like to know from the Finance minister or the Postmaster General what has been the average cost of the commissions which have been appointed since this government took office to investigate charges of political partisanship against postmasters and postmistresses.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: These commissions are appointed on the same terms as set forth in the order in council that was passed during the regime of Sir Robert Borden after a conference between him and the then leader of the opposition. If charges of political partisanship are preferred, commissions issue. My memory is that the sum paid is twenty dollars per day. The Postmaster General, of course, has nothing to do with the issue of these commissions. They are issued by the government as a whole. Should charges of political partisanship be made and sent forward to any minister, he submits them to council, and a commission is issued by council accordingly.

What provision is made for the payment of the commissioners holding these investigations up to the end of the present fiscal year? How are they being paid, and what provision is being made for that purpose?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I cannot answer that question.
Evidently there is no provision in the supplementary estimates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No. I do not think any accounts have come in as yet.
It is an over-expenditure, and according to the principle laid down by the Prime Minister the other day, no overexpenditures should be ohargeable to next year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is no over-expenditure in the department. This sum will take care of any expenditures of the department to the end of the present fiscal year.

I am well aware of that, but there must be an over-expenditure in the Post Office Department to meet the very numerous investigations that are going on now, and have been going on for the last couple of months at least. According to the principle laid down by the Prime Minister, the other day, there should not be any overexpenditure in any department. But I cannot see that any provision is being made in the estimates either through the Justice department or the Post Office Department or any other department for that purpose.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will ascertain and let
the hon. gentleman know.

I wish to refer to a
matter which I called to the attention of the Minister of Justice the other day, and concerning which I have had no further reply from him. At that time I called his attention to the fact that some of the departments -I mentioned particularly the Post Office Department-had been sending out circular letters to officials enclosing an affidavit and calling upon the official to sign the affidavit to the effect that he had not been guilty of any acts of political partisanship. The letter also went on to intimate that if the official did not sign and return the affidavit, his dismissal would be proceeded with. I asked the Minister of Justice if he would look into the matter, and, if these letters were being sent out, take steps to bring the matter to the attention of the various departments and see that the sending out of such letters was discontinued, for the obvious reason that it is directly contrary to the practice which has existed, and to which my right hon. friend the Prime Minister has referred. The principle has been clearly laid down that except where there is a certificate by a member of parliament cases of political partisanship shall be tried and investigated in the regular way, and that the ordinary principles shall apply that a man is presumed innocent until proved guilty, and is not called upon to make an extraordinary affidavit of this kind. The Minister of Justice promised the other day that he would look into the matter and bring it to the attention of the departments, but I have not had any further word about it.
Even at this late hour and so near the Easter recess I feel that this matter is of sufficient importance to bring to the attention of the committee because I am satisfied that a number of these letters have gone out. It seems to me that it is not fair to the civil servants to put them in any such position and they should know the true situation at once otherwise the whole service will feel that they are under suspicion iby being called upon, as I said a moment ago, to prove themselves innocent instead of the usual procedure being followed of their being presumed innocent until found guilty. I want to put on record a copy of the letter which has been sent out. It is addressed to various postmasters, and reads:
Supply-Post Office

Dear Sir,
Representations have been made to the department to the effect that during your term of office as postmaster you have been guilty of acts of political partisanship. It is provided in the Civil Service Act that any government employee who is guilty of political partisanship in connection with any federal or provincial election shall be dismissed from the service.
As this charge has been made against you the Postmaster General is desirous of giving you an opportunity to state your side of the case.
The Prime Minister will note that there is no suggestion as to who makes the charges, but the intimation is that somebody has made representations to the department and the only trial is to require the civil servant to make an affidavit without knowing who charges him or the particulars of the charges.
That did not make any difference at all to the late government.

My hon. friend cannot
point to a single instance of a dismissal under the late government without an investigation and the regulations being carried out.

I can point to one in the
town of Leamington, Ontario. Let the exPost-master General look it up.

And I can point to one in
the town of Cambridge, New Brunswick.

My hon. friend is talking about cases that are not under the Civil Service Act at all. The Prime Minister has already intimated that the government are pursuing the course which has been laid down, and which has been the practice for a number of years.

This was a case under the
Civil Service Act.

So far as I know in no case where they have declined to act upon

them, unless they have written a communication in which they have admitted their guilt, has dismissal followed. I am bound to say to my hon. friend that there was a suggestion that if they declined to answer their action should be taken as an acquiescence and that they should be dismissed. Needless to say that suggestion was not acted upon?

And will not be acted
upon?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Was not and will not
be acted upon. There are cases in which, to save the expense of having a commission with all the attendant troubles, and where it is well known that there has been partisanship on the part of the individuals charged, that communication has been sent. I thmk the form of that communication leaves much to be desired. I believe if a suspected person were advised that a charge had been made against him indicating that he had been guilty of partisanship and saying that it might be advisable for him to resign rather than put the country to the expense of an investigation, no objection could be taken. However, I wholly agree with what the hon. gentleman has said. Strangely enough in the Civil Service Act reference has been made to both provincial and federal elections. I never knew just why provincial elections were mentioned in the statute, but the statute as it reads makes the incumbent of an office appointed under the act guilty of partisanship if he takes part in either a provincial or a federal election. That is why the word "provincial" is put in the statue. I think hon. gentlemen opposite can rely upon there being not attempt to treat unfairly those who are charged with partisanship, and certainly no effort will be made to relieve them of their positions because by mere silence they are regarded as acquiescing in charges made against them.

I want to say to my right hon. friend that we appreciate the assurance he has given. One thing further I would like to say: I suggest that in a letter of this kind it is not quite fair for a superior to suggest to a subordinate that it is advisable for him to do so and so. That is to say, I think that the farthest one can go is to say that the charges have been made and if those charges are not admitted an investigation will be held.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend would
not consider it as at all improper to say, "If you regard these charges as being warranted, your resignation will be in order," or something to that effect?

I submit not. I think the official is entitled to be told what the procedure is and the principles which have been laid down here, and it would be left to him to decide the course he wished to take rather than being advised by a superior. I suggest to my right hon. friend that the word "advisable" be left out.

In view of the procedure indicated I would like to take this opportunity of putting in an early plea for forgiveness of one particular postmaster. I never have been in favour of allowing a man's politics to interfere with his right of being a postmaster, and I would not like to see it happen in the future. The postmaster to whom I refer was the campaign manager for my opponent.
Oh, oh.

While we are on this matter perhaps it would save a great deal of trouble and time if the Prime Minister would make an authoritative statement with respect to complaints made by members of parliament asking that public officers be removed from office. He might give an outline of what these complaints must contain, and just how far such statements of members of parliament should be taken. I would ask the Prime Minister to go one step further than he has already gone when answering the question of my hon. friend from Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) and explain the custom in respect to the question I have asked.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman think at this hour of the night it is desirable his question should be answered? If some of these estimates do not pass there will be no cheques for those requiring relief, and I would remind hon. members opposite that the hour is now within a few minutes of eleven o'clock. In the main estimates these matters will again be traversed at greater length and perhaps we might save a lot of trouble and expense if my hon. friend's question was allowed to stand.

The only reason for
taking time with regard to this question is that when people get these letters they become panicky. They seem to think they are slated to be dismissed anyway, whether they are guilty or not, and therefore since they do not understand what their rights are they may do themselves an injustice which would be avoided if my right hon. friend would make a statement now. It would not take long for him to do so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have made a statement.
Supply-Post Office

I would ask my right hon. friend to make a statement with regard to
complaints by members of parliament.

I know of an instance in the constituency of North Battleford where the procedure described by my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth was actually followed. The man resigned when he received this threatening letter.
An hon. MEMBER . He must have been guilty.

He says he is not guilty, and personally I do not think he is. A petition has gone to the department asking that the man be restored to his position. In the event of the resignation of a man followed by a petition and an investigation to learn whether or not that man is guilty of partisanship, will an investigation be conducted and the man be restored to his position if it is proved that he is innocent?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Perhaps the committee
will recall that this matter was thoroughly threshed out last year in connection with a case in which the then Solicitor General had laid a charge of partisanship. The man was found not guilty of partisanship and it was determined by the Civil Service Commission that there was no power to restore the man to his position.
There was no question of the man having been found guilty or not guilty?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He was removed.
He was removed. But the right hon. gentleman said he was not found guilty of partisanship. There was no finding.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
He was charged with
partisanship.
And dismissed on the word of a member of parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And the evidence indicated that there had been a mistake.
To whom did the evidence indicate that? To the minister, not to the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
judicially was satisfied.
I do not think any one was.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Then we will withdraw the question of his being satisfied. But it was determined by the Civil Service Commission that once a man resigns his position, even though he may not desire to do so, or once he is removed from his position, he cannot, though he vindicates himself thereafter, be

restored to that position. That has been the finding in that regard. I tried to assert that it was an improper appreciation of the position, but they satisfied me that, as the law stands, they were right.
Is that the infallible justice of the crown?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, under the statute.

There is a misapprehension. Where an official is dismissed for cause he cannot re-enter the service, even if he qualifies under examination. But where an official resigns he has the right, a vacancy being created, to apply again and undergo the qualifying examination.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Certainly.
But the right hon. gentleman's statement did not leave that impression.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes. He has the right to apply, the same as any other citizen, but he starts all over again.
He loses his standing.
Mr. Chairman,-
Let us get through.

I have a right to address the committee without back-benchers interfering. We do not hear much from the front benches but a good deal from the back. There is in my riding a case which comes within the discussion that has been going on for the last fifteen or twenty minutes. There is in a small village in my riding a postmaster who received one of these letters read by the hon. member sitting in front of me, and also the form of an affidavit, and I advised him neither to sign the affidavit nor to resign. I took the ground that until that postmaster was proven guilty he was innocent. I also took the matter up with the Postmaster General and received a letter in reply. I am sorry I have not that letter before me. It is in my room.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It is now almost eleven o'clock, and if the committee desires to proceed beyond that hour it can do so only by unanimous consent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I was going to ask, Mr. Chairman, that the ordinary rule of moving the Speaker back to the chair be dispensed with by unanimous consent, and that we sit another half hour.
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is the motion carried?

Supply-Post Office

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Is that acceptable?
I would be willing to agree to it if I got my statement. Otherwise no unanimous consent; I object.

The letter, if I remember it-if I am wrong the Postmaster General, if he is permitted to answer me, will correct me

intimated that the fact that I had advised this postmaster not to resign or to sign the affidavit was really evidence of guilt.
Hear, hear.

"Hear, hear," my hon. friend says. Surely no hon. member in this house will say that because a postmaster refuses to resign, or refuses to sign an affidavit, he has been proven guilty. And mark you, in this particular case I tried to find out the names of the parties who laid the information, and apparently there has been no information laid at all. It is only a matter of rumour and hearsay.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Has he been dismissed?

He has not been dismissed, and in his letter the Postmaster General stated that if the postmaster in question had made up his mind that he would not resign, or if he would not sign the affidavit, a commission would have to be appointed to take evidence. I do not object to that, but if this is done the names of those who laid the complaint must be made known and a full investigation instituted. But I claim that to ask this postmaster, or any other postmaster, to allow himself to be clubbed into a resignation, or clubbed into signing the affidavit before anything is proven, is at least not British justice.
Is the Postmaster General prepared to give the name of the informant, or the names of those who complained against the postmistress at Vermilion Bay, Ontario?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The case was investigated, I believe, at a public hearing and a report made.

I am asking whether the
Postmaster General will give us the name of the person who laid the complaint in connection with the matter in the first instance.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That has been held to
be unnecessary in cases that occurred under the late administration and the one previous to that, provided there is an investigation in which the accused makes his defence. Then the matter can be discussed in parliament in the light of the investigation and report.

Now that we have decided
to sit an extra hour, surely the Prime Minister will give the explanation for which I asked and which he said he could not give by reason of the shortness of time. I am not endeavouring to stir up trouble, I am trying to get from him his interpretation of the nde which has always been followed-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not always.
-that a public officer may be dismissed on the personal certificate of a member of parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The matter was placed
on Hansard last year by the Postmaster General, and I should not care to make a statement without looking up the strict terms of the order in council. My memory of it might be defective as to the exact words used. I might send for Hansard, or if my hon. friend would do so himself, he would find the statement to which I refer. I shall be glad at the proper time to accommodate the hon. gentleman in that regard.

I do not wish to interrupt anyone but I rise to a point of order. According to the rules, the house cannot sit after eleven o'clock except by unanimous consent. I am not going to make trouble or threaten the government, but I wish to have a satisfactory answer to my question regarding the building of the station at Riviere du Loup, and I have-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: What is the point of order?
The point of order is that the house cannot sit after eleven o'clock except by unanimous consent.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I nde that the house is not sitting; it is the committee, and there was unanimous consent.

No, Mr. Chairman; you
have not mine.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
I said that a condition was to be fulfilled.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point of order has been decided. If the hon. member is not satisfied he can appeal to the committee.

In view of the statement which the Prime Minister has made, and the concurrence he has given in the terms he has used regarding the letter I have read, I wish to ask him whether instructions will be given
Supply-Post Office

to withdraw these letters and if desired to have amending letters written omitting the objectionable portions to which I have referred. He will agree that the letters are not such as should go to civil servants.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think the Postmaster General has already directed that no further letters of that kind are to be sent out.
That is not quite enough.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He certainly is not writing further letters to the people to whom they have been sent, but that form of letter has been discontinued.

I express the opinion
deferentially that that should be done., and I think my right hon. friend, who understands as well as anyone in this house, and perhaps better than most, the general principles which govern the investigation of charges, knows that is not a letter which ought to be allowed to stand as coming from a senior to a subordinate. I want to ask my right hon. friend if he will not have these letters withdrawn and cancelled, and such letters sent out if desired as are appropriate under the circumstances.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I shall be glad to look into the matter.

The other matter I had in mind was with regard to what my hon. friend from Quebec South said. Can we at least have this understanding, that dismissals will not be made on the so-called certificate of a member of parliament unless the member of parliament certifies that the acts of partisanship are to his personal knowledge?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As I said a moment ago, whatever has been the practice heretofore has been observed. The exact procedure I do not carry in mind at the moment, hence I do not care to make a statement without looking up the order in council to find the exact language.
I should like to ask the Prime Minister what attitude the various ministers will follow in cases where complaints are made by defeated candidates of acts of political partisanship.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They are not dismissed without an investigation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The Prime Minister referred to an order in council a moment ago. Does he mean the order in council which was in force under the previous administration? That is satisfactory if that is what he meant.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is what I mean.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.

Relief of fire sufferers at Hebertville Station, Quebec-governor general's warrant of September 26, 1930, $5,000.
I should like to ask, purely out of curiosity, how it happens that the federal government has come to the relief of fire sufferers. Is this something new?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, it is not something new. The province of Quebec made an appropriation and an application was made to the administration for assistance. It was found that in similar cases sums had been paid by previous administrations, and accordingly this amount of $5,000 was paid.

The circumstances must
have been very unusual.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the place was wiped out.
It seems very extraordinary that the federal government should pay sufferers from fire. Surely the circumstances would have to be very exceptional.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is exactly the position I took.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Relief of pensioners - governor general's warrant of November 20, 1930, $275,000.

On this item I should like
to say a word which I assure hon. members will not be of a controversial or political nature. In common with a great many others who are interested in returned soldiers and in pensions I am beginning to fear that the pension legislation of last session may not be as effective as those who took part in the preparation of it had anticipated. I do not propose for a moment to discuss what may have been the reasons which bring this legislation almost face to face with failure. It may be and probably is due to the fact that there were inherent defects in the legislation; it may be that the proper precautions were not taken to see that it was carried out in every particular.
That is not the question I wish to raise to-night, however. I wish to ask the Prime Minister to consult with his colleagues, with the members of these boards and with the officers of the department during the recess with a view to some attempt being made to modify or alter or if necessary to crap the legislation in order that we may be able to dispense that justice to the returned soldiers that those of us who served on the committee as well as the members of this house hoped we were dispensing throught the legislation of last year. I am not making this statement by way of criticism; I think the right hon. gentle-

Supply-Governor General's Warrants
man understands that, and I think those members of the house who were on the parliamentary committees of last year will understand the position I take. I make this suggestion in order that something may be done at the earliest possible moment to remedy any defects which may exist in the present system so. that we shall not be face to face, in a short time, with an agitation throughout the country which might make it impossible for the members of this house and the government to deal with the situation without taking radical steps in the way of granting pensions in a wholesale fashion, which none of us desire.
I am asking the Prime Minister particularly to direct his attention to this very serious and urgent matter of national importance during the recess so that he may come to parliament after Easter with some solution for it. Personally I may say that whatever experience I have acquired during the past few years in dealing with this question is at the disposal of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Pensions and National Health. I do not propose now, any more than I did in the past, to deal with this matter in any political way whatever. I have already offered privately to cooperate with the minister. I make that offer again and I sincerely hope, in the interests of the country at large as well as in the interests of the government and of the opposition, that something may be done in the shortest possible time to deal with this matter.

I should like to say
just a word in support of the hon. member who has just spoken. No one who has worked with the hon. member can help realizing that in dealing with this subject he has been indeed absolutely free from any taint of partisanship or politics. I have worked with the hon. member many years in connection with this matter and always, as chairman of our committee and as its representative here in the house, he has been absolutely fair.
I have placed a number of questions on the order paper, having that same situation in mind, because with many others who have been interested in the matter, I am impressed by its urgency. Possibly there are defects in the legislation, but certainly consequences have arisen already which are going to make for great difficulty in the very near future. I too would ask the Prime Minister and his colleagues to look into the question, and like the hon. member who has just spoken, if there is anything I can do I shall be only too glad to do it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In answer to the hon.
gentlemen who have just spoken I should say that the same considerations which have influenced their judgment and brought about the statements they have made have been apparent to the government for some time, and already the matter is being looked into. We shall be very glad indeed to avail ourselves of their mature advice and generous assistance.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Removal, ordnance stores from Ross Rifle factory' buildings, Quebec-(governor general's warrant of November 27, 1930), $26,000.

Mr. Chairman, if the Prime Minister will give me the undertaking that at some future time 1 shall be permitted to discuss this matter, I will be prepared to do so and shall be glad to point out to the house and to tin country what I consider has been a senious defect in administration and what has been very nearly a scandal in the Department of National Defence. However, I have neither the time this evening nor the necessary information to carry on this discussion. If the right hon. gentleman and the Minister of National Defence are willing that the matter be discussed when the main estimates are being considered, I shall have no objection to this item being passed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will have that opportunity, but I would point out to him that this probably comes within the terms of the order in council passed on January 9, 1923.
No, it does not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is thought that the terms of that order are broad enough to cover this matter.

If the terms of that order passed in 1928 had been broad enough to cover this matter I do not think a governor general's warrant would have been necessary. Under the terms of that order in council an amount of $100,000 was placed in the estimates to cover the removal of the Ross rifle factory. I take it that the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) or the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) advised the right hon. gentleman that the terms of the order did not cover the removal of stores at this time and that therefore it was necessary to issue a governor general's warrant. However, that is a matter to be discussed at the proper time. There will not be an item in the main estimates covering the removal of these stores,

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Quite so.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Relief of pensioners (governor general's warrant of March 6, 1931), $75,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with the permission of my right hon. friend I would like to comment upon certain of his remarks which appear on page 408 of Hansard, as follows:
This committee, being anxious to retain some semblance of integrity with respect to its dealings, is now legalizing the unwarranted acts of those who made certain expenditures because they say they were instructed to do so.
I hope that my right hon. friend did not mean to imply that the alleged unwarranted acts related to the previous administration. He must realize that many of the expenditures which he classes as unwarranted because they are included in these estimates to which his remarks refer, as for instance the Welland canal item of $2,000,000, were due to actions of his own administration with which the previous government had no connection whatever.
It is desirable at this time to make very clear the course which should be followed in order to secure effective parliamentary control over expenditures. In this connection I would say to my right hon. friend that what he has said with respect to civil servants is equally applicable to the ministry as a whole. The right hon. gentleman quoted from the report of The" Auditor General as follows- the quotation will be found at page 409 of Hansard:
The over-expending of appropriations has the effect of lessening parliamentary control over expenditures and, although in very exceptional eases it may have to be permitted, the practice is to be deprecated and means should be taken to prevent it.
Most if not all of the items we have had under discussion cover matters of overexpenditure. My right hon. friend continued as follows:
The responsibility is, as the Auditor General says, with the accountants of the departments, and if parliamentary control of appropriations is to be maintained except under very exceptional conditions that may sometimes prevail, it follows that discipline must be applied, or the whole system will be wrecked for if accountants and deputy ministers under the control of ministers may make beyond parliament appropriations, expenditures amounting to $1,000,000, they can do it to the amount of $5,000,000 or $10,000,000.

At page 411 the right hon. gentleman continues:
The Auditor General directs attention to what must be painfully apparent to everyone. It means that you substitute the minister and an accountant for parliament, because the money has gone and there was no appropriation for it.
And again at the bottom of the page:
I think an effort should be made to make it possible for each department to live within its appropriation. If not, some men will lose their positions. That is all I have to say.
I agree with my right hon. friend's point of view as here presented. What I would suggest respectfully is that what is true as regards the permanent officials of the government in the matter of preventing overexpenditure and not going beyond appropriations is applicable in even greater measure, and applies with greater force to the ministry itself. There should not be occasion again to have to draw attention to the fact that a ministry of its own volition has exceeded an appropriation or has permitted expenditures to be incurred for which no appropriation by parliament has been made.
I wish to join with the Prime Minister in seeking effectual control by parliament over expenditure. I believe that to be one of the most important functions of parliament, effectively to control the expenditures of the country. This can be done only by restricting expenditures to such amounts as have been provided for by appropriations made by parliament in the regular way.
May I add this word in regard to governor general's warrants. I have stated frequently that the government might have obtained a governor general's warrant for the purpose of unemployment relief. I hope that my right hon. friend and members generally will appreciate that when I made that statement I had reference to the fact that an Imperial conference was to be held last year in London and that it was recognized by everyone that the Prime Minister and his colleagues would wish to attend and should attend that conference. Under the circumstances it was hardly possible to have parliament meet in time to-pass the appropriations necessary for the year and a governor general's warrant would, I think, have served the purpose as regards-what was necessary for unemployment relief. I would not like it to be thought for one moment that I favoured the issuing of such warrants except in circumstances which are most exceptional or where the deferring of the meeting of parliament can be justified only by circumstances which are apparent to everyone as reasonable.

Supply-Governor General's Warrants

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is very seldom that the right hon. gentleman and myself agree, but this is a matter upon which we do agree and have agreed for many years. I do not agree wholly with his view with respect to governor general's warrants, for I do not believe that circumstances arising within an administration constitute a necessity for the issuance of such warrants. There is that difference between us. There are circumstances such as the destruction of a bridge, the burning of a building or the establishment and maintenance of the government itself where warrants should be issued, but there must be satisfactory evidence to warrant this action being taken. May I say this to the committee: These estimates have been introduced for the purpose of enabling the government to start with a clean sheet. That is, where over-payments have been made, and some of them attributable to the present administration, as the right hon. gentleman says, on the 31st day of this month, that is to-day, if these estimates pass, there will then be established a clean sheet and a new leaf will be turned on the book enabling the government to do what, I believe, should be done by all governments, namely, to maintain its expenditures within its appropriations. I am sorry to say to the committee that despite the efforts that I made personally, there is one item that has not been brought into the house. It is a small item, it is true, but it was overlooked by the minister in charge. This shows how difficult it is to follow these matters. As I say, it is not a large sum, but we could not insert it in the estimates without a new message which could not be secured. An effort will be made, commencing the new year on April 1, to keep expenditures within the appropriations and we shall ask the house and the country to judge us by our performance in the light of the statement of the principle which, I submit, should govern our actions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am anxious
that the clean sheet of the right hon. gentleman, when we see it next year, shall not have any spots upon it. For that reason I should like to draw his attention to what I believe caused the confusion last evening when we were discussing the unprovided items. They do not relate to the fiscal year in which the supplementary estimates are being presented; they relate to the year previous. As a consequence I say that despite my right hon. friend's good intentions, when we are discussing the estimates at this time next year, he will find he will be obliged to bring in further unprovided items for this 22110-33i
very fiscal year 1930-31, that is to say, for the fiscal year which Jie now thinks he has cleaned off so completely. He will find that the Auditor General will present to him a report to the effect that several of the departments have not paid some outstanding accounts; that they have been overlooked by ministers or deputy ministers or accountants, and he will ask that an item be inserted in the estimates to cover those unprovided amounts. I hope with my right hon. friend that the amounts will be small, but I am afraid that despite his efforts and good intentions one corner of the sheet will have a spot upon it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman has had more experience than I, and I daresay his suggestion is sound; but the ministers, if they were permitted, would tell the committee that they have been asked and asked again as to any over-expenditures, and a very earnest effort has been made to cover every item up to the end of the present fiscal year. I hope-and I thank the right hon. gentleman for extending the information to the government-that such a condition as he suggests will not arise.
Has the Auditor General been asked not to over-spend in his own department?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am bound to say that that step has been taken.

speakerposition: stagedirection

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The ex-Minister of the Interior asks why under this estimate the moneys may be spent prior to the 31st day of May. In the accounting of the railways, the very difficulties that have been experienced in government have arisen, and the auditors desire that this sum which is now known to exist, but all of which has not been audited and settled in the ordinary course of transactions, should be made available for the purposes up to within a reasonable time. The principal reason is that they have no money with which to pay this now and that they may not get the money for some little time, because we have to provide it. It is rather a large sum of money, so they suggest that if the 31st May be fixed, this would enable them, without question, to treat the accounts in the manner I have indicated.

I suppose the right hon. gentleman realizes that the statement he has just given to the committee is rather extraordinary. This is the first time in my experience I have seen a supply bill used to amend the Audit Act. The matter is a serious one. The Audit Act is the root and basis of our financial structure and I do not believe it is proper to use it in this manner.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Why?

I will tell the right hon. gentleman why. I wonder that the Prime Minister who, I think, is more familiar than I am with the Audit Act, realizes that section 49 of that act not only enables the government to spend all moneys voted by parliament on the main or supplementary estimates, but also authorizes the government by order in council to extend the time of any such payment for exactly the period he is now asking parliament to extend the fiscal year, namely, from April 1 to May 31. This is provided under section 49 of the Audit Act, if there are any payments pending that have not been specifically and in exact amount provided for by this vote-though the vote as I said a minute ago is extremely explicit, though it is couched in precisely the same
language as the main estimate for the capital expenditure of the Canadian National Railways. This is the first time these means have been used to modify, by a supply bill, an act cf parliament. I think the Prime Minister has the power under section 49 of the Audit Act and strongly advise or request or beg him to strike out of the supply bill the words-
Notwithstanding the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, this appropriation shall not lapse before May 31, 1931.
I think the right hon. gentleman has the power to do that under the Audit Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The question raised by the
hon. member for Rimouski is one that has been considered by the government. Section 39 of the act provides the method whereby it may be done. It provides:
When any sum of money has been granted to His Majesty by parliament to defray expenses for any specified public service, the governor general may, from time to time, under his sign manual, countersigned by a member of the treasury board, authorize and require the Minister of Finance to issue out of the moneys in his hands, appropriated for defraying the expenses of such service, the sums required, from time to time, to defray such expenses, not exceeding the amount of the sum so voted or granted.
This means that the Minister of Finance must send the recommendation to council; secondly, that it must be considered by council; thirdly, when adopted, the governor in council releases it; and fourthly, letters of credit are issued with respect to it.
Will the right hon. gentleman read the second paragraph of section 49?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have it beside me, but 1 do not want to take up time in reading it. This is not our money for the purpose of expending it as we please. It is required to meet specific deficits in the operation of the railway; and their audit is made, not ours. All we do is to pass it out of our hands under the circumstances to which I have alluded. I desire, inasmuch as it may be difficult under present conditions to raise the sum of money required in a moment or two, that we and the railway company both should have an extension of time until the 31st of May in which to deal with the matter. It is unusual, I admit. It has been done only once before, but that was on an occasion somewhat similar to this. If the committee thinks that the public interest is not being as well served in this way as in some other, I am content; but it might result in the sum of money not being made available at all.

Supply-Loans to Canadian National
The usual practice is to borrow from the bank when you have authority.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Suppose the bank will not lend it; that is the trouble.
I did not think that the bank would refuse to lend money to the government.

I am not criticizing; I am simply calling the attention of the house to what is being done. I am firmly convinced that you have the power to exercise your rights under section 49 of the act. I would like the Prime Minister to consider for a moment the four modes provided for raising these loans; first, by direct loan; second, by loans from the public; third, by guarantees; fourth, by temporary borrowing. More than that, these four methods must be approved by the governor in council. So you have there all the necessary machinery to raise the money immediately, and in addition you can provide money by governor general's warrant. It has been the opinion of the committee in the past that the way in which we have allowed these loans to be floated by the Canadian National perhaps has not been the proper method, and I think that when the question of adjusting the general finances of the Canadian National oomes up for consideration, there will be a considerable body of opinion that the present method is not the proper way of doing it. I certainly believe that you have all the necessary power under this appropriation and under the Audit Act, without creating this precedent. That is only my opinion, but I felt in duty bound to express it.

speechtext: This is not the kind of case that is meant by that at all.

This is a vote made by parliament for a particular purpose. The money may eventually go to the Canadian National Railway, but for the present it goes to the government and is paid out by government cheque.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Surely my hon. friend does not mean that. This is a credit not for the government but for the railway, and so far as we are concerned this is the last time we propose to submit it in that form. I repeat, this is not a credit to the government; it is merely a credit to the railway company.

My hon. friend will admit that the government can secure the money from parliament for that particular purpose as for any other purpose. There is really no difference. The government could not, of course, divert the money from the railway, but the government is responsible for raising the money for the railway and passing it on to them. I cannot understand why the government should require any extra time. There may be reasons why the railway may require extra time.
