speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
His words I took to imply that, because he said, at page 355 of Hansard:
That has been done before, and the reason is that the obligations have been created. The bills are not all in and will not be in by Tuesday next, and therefore it is desired to have until May 31 to audit the accounts and make the payments. When the bill comes before the house, if the house thinks such a provision-which is purely a matter of bookkeeping to facilitate the operations of the company-should not be there, it can be dealt with later. The estimate does not bind the house.
I took those words to mean that the Prime Minister would defer to the wishes of a considerable body of opinion in the house if it expressed itself as being opposed to this particular course. May I say to my Tight hon. friend that our desire in this matter is to further what he a moment ago expressed himself so strongly as favouring, namely effectual parliamentary control over expenditures. The Audit Act relates to the payment of accounts. My right hon. friend drew attention, in a way that perhaps the house did not observe, to the fact that what is being asked is something more than permission to make payment of expenditures already made. What he is seeking, or perhaps I should say what the officers of the company appear to be seeking through this provision, is authority not only to have expenditures already made regularized, or payment made of services already performed, which is all that we should be asked to sanction, but that payment may be made of obligations incurred but which are 'not in the nature of services already performed and payment with respect to which as a consequence may be made only at some future time. That is a wrong principle for the house to sanction. The whole purpose of the Audit Act is to see that accounts, where services have been performed, are paid within a certain time. If we pass this item in the form here
proposed we will be opening the door to am entirely new principle in government auditing which will mean that the government, despite an aot of parliament passed in order to prevent anything of the kind, will be saying to a corporation that it may incur obligations today but that it need not fulfil the obligations within a given time, but may make payment of them within several months after the fiscal or financial year has elapsed. My right hon. friend used the following words:
Perhaps my right hon. friend will observe that there is a provision making this estimate available until the end of May, although practically all sums have been expended already.
With respect to all sums already expended no objection is being taken, and without the clause to which exception has been taken all such sums will be paid. But my right hon. friend adds the following:
.... or the liabilities have been incurred for which the money is required.
I do not think that we should be asked to repeal a part of the audit act so as to allow payment of liabilities which have been incurred to be made beyond a period of time never contemplated when parliament was surrounding the expenditure of public monies with the safeguard which the audit act places about it. On the following page my right hon. friend said:
The amounts covered by these estimates have been spent, or the deficits have arisen, but all the bills have not come in as yet.
The purpose of an audit is to see that accounts are sent in within a certain time and that the audit will cover expenditures which have been made, but that it shall not be. extended so as to permit commitments to be made to-day to be met several months after the termination of the financial year. When during the special session the government introduced the Unemployment Relief bill it was pointed out that it was desirable that the provisions of that act should expire with the fiscal year. However, my right hon. friend then adopted a new method of permitting payment of public moneys for a period beyond the fiscal year. I should like to read his words as they are found in Hansard, page 164:
However. I would add by way of amendment that any moneys that have not been expended, or that are not liable to be paid under obligations already created, shall lapse on March 31,
1931.
Upon that occasion my right hon. friend was introducing an entirely new principle with respect to appropriations by this parliament. He was not appropriating moneys required to be expended simply within the year but he

was appropriating sums of money which might continue to be paid out long after the fiscal year had expired, running on possibly inde-. finitely into another fiscal year so long as the obligation might be said to have been incurred within the fiscal year in which the act was passed. That is a very serious departure and a departure which is being emphasized and repeated by What is being proposed at the present time. I would humbly suggest to my right hon. friend that he defer to the wishes of a very considerable number, if not a majority in this house, and adhere strictly to the provisions of the audit act with respect to all government financing and particularly financing with respect to the National Railways.
Possibly I may be permitted at this point to add a word which may help to regularize matters and at the same time help to avoid the embarrassment my right hon. friend fears. Undoubtedly he will be asking parliament for a percentage of the main estimates immediately following the Easter recess. If he finds that the railway company is going to be embarrassed through not having the amount of money that is needed to meet obligations which will be coming due in the new fiscal year, and some of which may be included in the amount which is set forth in the present estimate of $11,410,400.85 I think I can say to him on behalf of the opposition that we will offer no objection to an estimate applicable to the new fiscal year which he may present at the same time to make good that particular difference so that there will be no embarrassment occasioned the company. Under the circumstances I hope my right hon. friend will feel that he might properly ask the chairman to strike out the. clause which if it remains would oblige us in connection with this estimate to all intents and purposes to repeal an important provision of the audit act and establish a precedent which I believe he would greatly regret immediately it had been established.

-for these particular purposes. So far as I am concerned this is a matter of supreme indifference. As a Minister of Finance I am endeavouring to discharge my duties and to pioceed in fairness to the corporation for which this money is voted. If hon. gentlemen opposite desire to take a different attitude they may do so. However, I have stated my position. I believe I am taking the position that any lawyer or any business man would take, namely: Can the public interest be adversely affected? Is some audit to be held? Is some supervision of accounts to be made? If the answer to these questions is in the affirmative there can be no possible harm done to the public interest; if otherwise, some harm might be done. When I hear hon. gentlemen opposite talk about departure from precedent I say, "Certainly, that is what laws are for." That is what parliaments are for-to make precedents when occasion arises. The fiscal year of this railway company ended December 31. We have now reached the end of March and they require $11,000,000 to meet the deficit in operations for the year ending December last. Through this estimate we are given the opportunity to provide money until May 31 under the same sanction, with the same provision and the same audit, and it is idle to talk of any other feasible means being provided to supervise this expenditure.
Now, if my right hon. friend thinks that in the public interest this item should be stricken out I am content; take it out. I am not at all concerned about it. I will say however that it will work a great injustice on the people concerned; it will cause needless hardship and needless delay, and parliament with its plenary power should see to it that as little inconvenience as possible is caused to businessmen in the discharge of their obligations.

speechtext: I am talking about that; that does not give it any sanction. Surely the hon. gentleman knows that. The statute which he has been reading to-night, and to which he attaches so much importance, should inform him of that. I believe that in departmental accounting they have followed the custom of most businesses and accounted as liabilities those that come in up to within the first fortnight. Cheques issued up to April 11 would be ample for the purpose. Under the circumstances, the house will adjourn until tomorrow, when we shall dispose of the amendment. The committee may have an opportunity to think about it in the meantime. I have not been able to get it printed, but it merely provides that cheques may be issued up to April 11, 1931, and chargeable against the year ending March 31, 1931. Without that this would be a needless expenditure of labour.

subsubtopic: ACCEPTANCE OF PROPOSAL OF CANADIAN HIGH COMMISSIONER FOR MEETING IN LONDON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have to advise the house that I have received from the High

Royal Grain Commission
Commissioner in London a telegram which is dated at Rome and which reads in part as follows:
After days of discussion I submitted resolutions providing for conference of all exporting countries. Motion unanimously endorsed and representatives export countries organized conference last night. As Canada's representative I was selected permanent chairman. Invited conference to Canada and pressed strongly for acceptance. All expressed desire for Canada but felt distance and time made it impossible. As next best I suggested London with Canada House meeting place. Unanimously approved and conference meets there May 18.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: EXPECTED ARRIVAL IN CANADA OF SIR JOSIAH STAMP
speechtext:
A few days ago I promised that before the Easter recess I would make a short statement regarding the proposed commission that is to be appointed to look into matters connected with the grain trade. For some years past there has been prevalent amongst the agricultural class, especially the grain producers in western Canada, the opinion that the sale of grain futures was detrimental to the producer. There is also a certain body of public opinion that holds the exactly opposite view. It is regarded by the government as important that the question should be authoritatively determined. The government has asked the three western provinces to agree on the naming of a representative of the agricultural interests and the grain exchanges to name another, and the government has requested Sir Josiah Stamp, who is the chief executive officer of the London, Midland and Scottish Railway and who is regarded as one of the most eminent living economists, to come to Canada as chairman of that commission. Sir Josiah Stamp has consented to undertake the work, although it will entail some considerable inconvenience to him. He will sail this week, and if nothing happens to the contrary he will arrive in Ottawa about the ninth day of April. He will proceed west and determine with his colleagues the simple, single question:	Does
the sale of grain futures operate to the detriment of the producer? It is hoped that the finding of that commission will lay at rest the difficulties that have so long been present in the minds of agriculturists of western Canada.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) the other day made an observation with respect to a "Canada first" policy. Owing to the fact that there has been a sharp difference of opinion on this continent with respect to the desirability of maintaining markets for the sale of futures, it is believed that the purpose which we have in mind will be best served by securing the services of a chairman entirely removed from the scene of those conflicts of opinion on the American continent. Accordingly, Sir Josiah Stamp has been asked to come, and he has accepted the task.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

I should like to ask a question based on a report which appears in the Ottawa Journal of this morning, and in order to place my question properly before the house I beg leave to read an excerpt from the statement which appears in the Journal. The statement is headed:
Federal relief to be continued. Minister of Labour issues statement that money is available.
The words which purport to be a quotation from a statement of the Minister of Labour are as follows:
The statement in part concluded:	"No
portion of the moneys appropriated for the carrying on of improvement works throughout Canada, amounting to $68,980,999, will lapse until June 1 next in Ontario, and July 1 in all other provinces, by which time it is
Unemployment Relief

expected the public works authorized by municipal, provincial and federal authorities will have been carried to completion."
With reference to direct relief, the sum of $4,000,000 was specifically appropriated by order in council on September 26, 1930, to pay one-third of the expenditures of municipalities for direct relief where suitable work cannot be provided for the unemployed.
On March 8. 1931, another order in council set aside $4,000,000 for direct relief.
"The estimated expenditure for direct relief to March 31, 1931, is about one and one-half *nillion dollars," continues the statement. 'There, therefore, remains available from the federal government's contribution for direct relief, the sum of two and one-half million dollars, which, it is intended, shall be used f?r the purpose outlined so long as the municipalities and provinces who are under agreement with the federal authorities to each Dear one-third of the total cost, consider conditions ot relief measures necessary."
My question is:	Does the representative
of the Minister of Labour in the house know whether or not this statement was given to the press by the Minister of Labour, and is tho statement correct?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (for the Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The statement given by the Minister of Labour to the press, and which has just been read by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stitt), is correct. I do not think that the hon. members for Winnipeg yesterday intended, in making the statements they did, to create any false impression, but apparently they were themselves labouring under a false impression when they stated that at midnight the moneys would lapse and there would be no further expenditures, or words to that effect. The expenditure will go on in accordance with the plan outlined by the Labour department; the works which have been initiated will be carried to their conclusion, and the services of those who have been employed on these works will be continued.
To complete the minister s statement, would he explain why the extension is for one month less in the case of Ontario as compared with the other provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I can only state in reply that those arrangements were made with the provinces and with the municipalities, and I presume that it suited the purpose to have it so arranged.

I had been about
to rise, Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, to refer to the despatch which has just been quoted by my hon. friend from Selkirk. The statement as handed to the press by Senator Robertson also included a statement that the impression conveyed by our speeches [J. H. Stitt.)
yesterday was wholly misleading. After the words of the minister speaking for the Minister of Labour in this house (Mr. Gordon) there is perhaps no very great need for us to state that we did not intend to mislead the house in any way. We had had no statement before the one read to-day from any member of the government as to the real situation; and, let me add, in some of the provinces at least the date of the 31st of March was definitely fixed as the date beyond which relief would not be given. I am informed this morning by the department that that is an arrangement as between the provinces concerned and the municipalities. That may be so, but I had had communications from outside that the relief was being cut off on the 31st of March and that in a number of municipalities there were no funds with which to pay relief under the arrangement beyond the 31st of March. So I hope the house will accept my statement that we had no desire whatever to mislead the house with regard to the urgency of the situation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Before the bill reaches a stage beyond that of the committee of the whole may I remind the right hon. the Prime Minister that I asked for some information last night. I asked him to ascertain from the Minister of Labour (Senator Robertson) whether he gave to any publication, or to anybody on behalf of any one of these publications, an assurance that it would receive special consideration. My question refers to certain papers and journals enumerated by my right hon. friend and he said he would give me the information to-day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have explained to my right hon. friend that there are no such documents or communications, at least upon the public files. I was permitted to read a letter written by Senator Robertson to the Hon. Charles McCrea. It was a personal letter in answer to a personal and confidential communication. I cannot give to the house the information contained in that letter. As it makes no commitment so far as the government is concerned, and was a personal communication, obviously I cannot communicate its contents to the house.

Royal Assent

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My question was whether or not the minister had given an assurance to anybody, not merely a written communication, but an assurance that certain of these papers or any one of them would receive special consideration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: So far as I know the answer must be in the negative. As I intimated to my right hon. friend however that construction might be placed upon a personal communication. Obviously I was permitted to read the letter only as a personal communication between two gentlemen one of whom is not a member of this house and so far as I know is not connected with any newspaper.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My right hon. friend has referred to communications. I should like to know whether an assurance was given to anybody on behalf of a paper. Assurances can be given by a minister verbally as well as in writing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am sure that he did not. Mr. MACKENZIE KING: All right. Then I asked for some information in regard to printing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have that information before me. Officials of the Post Office Department state the only printing that was done was done through the King's Printer and not otherwise, and the only direct contract for printing was made with the King's Printer. The King's Printer, referring to the inquiry made by the right hon. gentleman, states in a memorandum which I have before me that the only printing order for the Post Office Department placed by or for the King's Printer with a London firm during the fiscal year 1930-31 was an order made under date of July 9, 1930, to Lawson and Jones, Limited, London, Ontario, for 274,500 arrow stickers, in English and French, for the mail service branch. This was a lithographic job. The work was duly executed and the account for $137.25 was approved and paid by cheque No. 3551 under date of August 29, 1930. So far as the records show that is the only evidence of any printing done in London, Ontario, which found its way to the Post Office Department.
